utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Good morning to everybody. May we hear the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. This is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And the appearances, please, for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Nicholas Koumjian, Ann Sutherland, and Ruth Karper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, Branko Lukic, John Ostojic, and Danilo Cirkovic to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning again. Before we start, may I ask, what is the real time estimate the Defence would need for today with the military expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. It's difficult to estimate, because of the exhibits we would hope to walk through, as the Court sees in front of them the exhibits that the General has examined and we hope to move into evidence. We hope that it would be rather short. His report, we believe, at least in my opinion, is complete. I hope to walk him through the report. Obviously we don't want to have him just read the report like other witnesses. So I will take as much time as the Court allows. I could short circuit it, I want to highlight several specific points relating to the time period specifically involving the attacks, the three within the ten days, as well as the detention centres. That's the highlight of it. So I can take as long or as little I guess as the Court permits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What would -- what did you yourself calculate in the moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The last calculation approximately two and a half hours. And that's paring it down to be perfectly candid. I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Absolutely, because what we have to do is we have to be aware that this expert is available only for two days, and during these two days, no extra hour or extra minute is possible because of other hearings and the absence of additional courtroom availability. What about the Prosecution? I know it's difficult to ask already at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I would estimate three to four hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So normally, it takes longer. Can we maybe resolve the problem already by trying not to tender the documents during the hearing, but doing this in a kind of package solution. Only the most important documents, no doubt, where you believe it's absolutely mandatory that the expert witness has to rely on or believes that he has to rely on and he has to draw our attention especially. But in general, I think it would be a waste of the precious time to do this exercise during his presence. Can we agree on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I believe so, Your Honour. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So let us hope that we can go through the final questions. And what -- has there been already the attempt to come to an agreement on the admission of documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No, we don't have the documents the Defence is proffering today. We have not received a list or copy of those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I'm a little bit taken by surprise seeing one, two, three, four -- I can't see them. It seems to be something like --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Nine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, nine files. What we received indeed was as a basis for this expert statement, one file with a number of documents and a list, and the formal motion to amend the list of exhibits. When I asked -- I referred only to those other documents where we didn't have the possibility to decide on the admission. Those documents tendered in the past are -- where we had already a motion on the amendment of the exhibit list. Did you come for these documents to any conclusion or agreement?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We will not object to the addition of those documents. Sorry, my microphone does not seem to be working. There it is now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This facilitates -- these documents there, may I ask, are they already 65 terred?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I believe 90 per cent of them are, Your Honour. If I can just explain, perhaps I will help the Court as well as the Office of the Prosecution. The three binders to the right in front of the Court immediately are actually the footnotes. The parties have all those exhibits because most of them, if not all of them, were tendered to us at one point or another. To the extent that there are additional documents as reflected in the report by the General, he specifically cites the 65 ter, and that document is enclosed within those three binders. The balance six binders include a compilation of materials that include different topic areas as reflected in the indictment, specifically there's police reports, which indicate on the issues of prevention and punishment; there's other military reports that the General did not use in his report, but nonetheless reviewed and may rely on depending, again, upon the questions, et cetera. I can't recall what the next volume is, but two volumes include various articles that the General reviewed in connection with the background of the events and for further support. All those articles are in the possession of the OTP, and I believe the Court, through our 65 ter submission and ultimate translation. I believe there's just a couple documents that are not included, but I think under the rules, the Court can take judicial notice of it, specifically the Geneva Convention, there's references in there that the General makes in his report, specifically if I recall, Article 25 of the report, and we would expect to be able to ask him questions relating to that because it goes to the issue of detention centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to explain, because it may require more time for us to prepare in cross-examination, we haven't received these documents before. Some of these footnotes cite 65 ter numbers. We originally received all of the Defence 65 ters, most of which were not translated. Some were. The translated -- complete translations, I believe we've only received up to Document 249. So we haven't received some of the documents that are 65 terred and footnoted in the Defence expert's report. We're ready to go today right now, but as soon as we can get the documents, the better for us to prepare our cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right. I understood this caveat. Therefore, I have to ask the Defence to conclude the examination-in-chief today, in the light of what you have said before and your own estimate. I think this is fair. It allows us, even though it's late, maybe to go through the documents during the afternoon, for those who have time to do this. But let's try. A final question: General Wilmot is still an acting general?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: As reflected in his CV, he's retired, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: To put it very simple: As a retired general, he's acquainted to be addressed as "General" or how?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I address him as "General," but it really doesn't matter. If the Court wants to address him as Mr. Wilmot, I don't think he would have an objection. I just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We have Only to be judicially correct, and for this purpose, therefore my purpose -- purpose of my question. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: One other --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: One other thing, if I may, to respond, I think there might be a confusion with the 65 exhibits. This is the first I hear that they only got up to 249. I know there has been some discussions with our case manager on that. When we submitted the 65 ter number and we raised Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. it in an oral motion an hour before the Court, the 65 ter Defence number exhibits, we filed the exhibit list on November 18th as the Court knows. We asked for the translation that was ultimately completed sometime in February, I believe, of this year. When we -- two weeks or a week before we got it completed, we received from the OTP a list of approximately 100 or so, and I think it was actually 150 exhibits that they have already previously translated, but not tendered. So we got that list from them. So they have in essence in their possession we believe most if not all of the exhibits that were previously tendered. But we welcome the opportunity to visit with them immediately afterwards and to resolve any concerns or problems that they have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I just suggest it be very simpler for us, if the Defence is providing the Court with a copy of the documents we receive the same copy, rather than making Ms. Karper try to collect the documents from among our 3 million pages of documents. If we just receive an extra copy of what the Defence gives the Court, it would be very helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: At the moment, we are with Document 249.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We actually have gotten the full translations through 249.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The same is true for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would like to begin as soon as possible, but Mr. Lukic has advised me he personally gave to the Court officer all the exhibits on our 65 ter list, not just up to 249 -- not the Madam Registrar, but the court officer -- Ms. Courtney Musser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Unfortunately, she fell ill, and there are some logistic problems, but we will find out as soon as possible. It's already a search and seizure under the way. So without further ado, may I ask the usher to escort the witness into the courtroom, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning, General Wilmot.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Welcome to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May we start with what you have in your hand, your solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, so help me God.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You are called as an expert witness by the Defence. Therefore, the floor is therefore for the Defence, Mr. Ostojic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: As you know, my name is John Ostojic, and along with Branko Lukic and our case manager Danilo Cirkovic, we represent Dr. Milomir Stakic. Today we're going to ask you a series of questions in connection with your report that was submitted to the Court on March 3rd, 2003. If at any time, sir, you do not understand my question, please inform me of the same, and I'll try to clarify the question so that you may fully understand and you may give us your complete answer. Fair enough?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: For the record, can you please give us your full name.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: It's Richard Wayne Wilmot, W-i-l-m-o-t.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you give us your date of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: December 28th, 1934.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Where do you presently reside?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: I reside in two places. Sedona, Arizona, and northern Arizona in the city of Phoenix depending on the weather.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, by way of background can you share with us your educational background, essentially the highest level of education that you attained, where, and when?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: I'm a graduate of Michigan State University, in east Lansing, Michigan, and I'm a graduate of the U.S. Army War College and the Industrial College of the Armed Forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Attached to your report is your curriculum vitae. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel and witness please break between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, General, they are translating what we are discussing and three languages are used in this Court. So to the extent -- and it's my fault, I should have warned you of this -- to the extent that it's possible, I'll try to pause, and I would like you to do so as well after my question before you provide us with an answer. Okay.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: As I was stating, is your curriculum vitae attached to your report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that's approximately six pages. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what year you graduated from the United States Army War College.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us a little bit about the college, what kind of courses are taken at that college.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: The United States Army War College is an institution of learning which is reserved for the people in the military, in the army in particular, who seem to be advancing through the ranks and are destined for higher command. The war college doesn't teach tactics; it doesn't teach training; it doesn't teach logistics. It teaches the use of the elements of national power. It talks about the United States at its highest level, at the executive level, the statutes and laws, the implications of warfare, and so it's a much more strategic college of instruction than some of the other institutions of the army. Wrapped up among the student body are people from the air force, people from the navy, people from the marine corps, people from the state department, people from the Central Intelligence Agency and other agencies of the government. The total student body is about 200 people. The course lasts for one year. The course is designed in such a way that each morning, a distinguished speaker, could be a foreign speaker, comes to the student body, presents a one-hour presentation, and then that person meets with his associates because normally he brings assistants with him or her, meets with the students to discuss the details of what was presented in the morning. So it's a rather thorough and interesting course. Also in that course, a student is allowed to travel, travel abroad, to work on issues and problems. The students are required to write papers, to offer ideas about the national structure and how it could be better used. And so it is a strategic look, it's a higher look, than one might do, one might accomplish at, for example, to command the General Staff College which deals with tactics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Koumjian, you were on your feet?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I've had five pages of the CV, but I see counsel is probably counting also the cover page, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That would be correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, you also studied at the Strategic Studies Institute in Oxford, England. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: That was part of the war college programme. I and five other Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. colleagues were preparing a paper that dealt with the first use of tactical nuclear weapons in Europe, if it ever came to that, and of course that has long since passed. In doing our research, we were invited to the institute at Oxford. And we spent several days there and met with some of the key curriculum people, used their libraries and reference materials. And it was a very, very interesting session and one that I appreciated very much at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough to highlight your additional training and graduation from other schools in the military as reflected on what's the third page of your CV. It's highlighted for us.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Well, the United States Army Command General Staff College, as I mentioned earlier, is an institution where you are taught tactics at a higher level, for example, division, corps, and at that time field army level. It's a course that is designed for majors and lieutenant-colonels primarily. It is a prestigious course. It's conducted at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas. It's one year in duration. And -- but it is much more tactical in nature than is the Army War College. In addition to that, you're taken out on field exercises. You participate in field training exercises as we call them. You're given examinations, and you go through a process of testing and examining throughout the year.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: The Industrial College of the Armed Forces, also one year course, and I took that by correspondence in this case. The Industrial College of the Armed Forces is also located in Washington, D.C. It's a logistics course, and it is rather strategic in nature also because it examines the issue of the fiscal policy of the country and works its way all the down to the more detailed issues of the logistical system of the Department of Defence and the military as it existed at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And then, sir, you list for us additional training and courses which you have taken during your career, correct, in the centre of page three of your curriculum vitae?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is there any one that you would particularly like to highlight or do you want to share with us, such as the Ranger school or the advanced quartermaster course?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Well, the Ranger school prepared me to do some special operations in the army. The Rangers school is -- I guess for those who don't understand the work "Ranger," substitute the word "commando." It's a very, very rigorous 9 to 12 week course with an extremely high dropout rate. We had 217 students start and 49 graduated about two months later, two and a half months later. So it's a very rigorous course and one that certainly tests your mental and physical limits, and if you're ever in stress or strain in a combat situation, I think it is a very, very good benchmark because you look back on that while you're in this physical stress or strain and you say to yourself, I can do this, I can do this, I've done it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, likewise on page 3 of your curriculum vitae, you highlight some of the honour and achievements that you've had. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Are there any in particular that you'd like to highlight for us?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: No, I think they are sort of standard honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to ask you, sir, can you tell us with respect to your employment after graduation from the United States Army War College, did you continue to be employed with the army?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: From what period to what period?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: From 1975 when I graduated until -- I believe I retired in 1982. It may have been late 1981, but in that time frame, about six years.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What's the highest rank that you achieved while you served in the United States Army time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: The rank of Brigadier-General.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, were you one of the youngest ever to achieve that rank?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: I don't know if I was one the younger ever, because I think in the early stages of the United States Army when you could buy a commission, people who were 20 years old were buying commissions if they came from a very wealthy and so-called aristocratic families and made themselves generals at an early age. But in this particular era and on the day I was promoted, I was the youngest flag officer in all the services and I stayed in that position for about six months until someone younger was promoted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you share with us if you were ever engaged in any military combat. Did you see action overseas anywhere?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I was in the 1st Infantry Division in Vietnam and saw combat with that division including the Tet defensive. And at that time I held the position of deputy intelligence officer for the division. I was also the military intelligence detachment commander, and I was a training officer for the long-range patrol for the division. And so I spent about a year in Vietnam and saw combat there with that organisation. And then strangely enough, as a civilian, I was involved in some combat in an assignment that I had where I actually travelled into Afghanistan and supported the Muslim rebels in their attempts to oust the Soviet army during its occupation and during the war in the mid-1980s in Afghanistan.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you highlight for us your employment history following your retirement from the army.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Once I retired from the army, I decided that I would like to do something slightly different, so I went to work for a very small organisation in London. And I moved to London and lived there for about I guess eight years. I was working for a company that was under contract to the Central Intelligence Agency. So while I was not on the rolls of the CIA, I was one of the worker bees that helped them accomplish the tasks that they assigned to that organisation. I stayed at that work for about eight years, as I mentioned, and then I returned to the United States. And let me see, I decided I wanted to build a house, so I could create my own construction company. Got a general contractor's license, built a house, built several spec -- what we call spec houses, the idea being to sell those houses for a profit. I discovered after building six or seven or those that I really didn't like that business, I found it kind of boring, so I dropped out of that. And I went into being a consultant. I formed a -- what I call a think tank, gathered up a group of professionals, and we started taking a look at infrastructure problems in third-world countries, the idea being that we wanted to go to those third-world countries and their governments and maybe get contracts to help them to improve their infrastructure using monies from anywhere we could find it, including U.S. State Department. At the same time, I publicised myself as a consultant and had various consulting activities and duties through that period of time. And then I was hired by an organisation called the Steele Foundation, which originally was a nonprofit company. It is now a for-profit organisation, and they are in the risk management business and crisis management business. And I became the CEO of that organisation, and then just recently I guess six or eight months ago, I downgraded myself to one of the executive directors because I found that being the CEO was more taxing in terms of using my time, and I didn't want to spend that amount of time with that organisation. So I still work with them, but now I'm called I think one of the managing directors or executive directors. I can't remember the exact title.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just give us a brief, if you will, overview of the Steele Foundation corporation in which you were the CEO. Was it broken up in different units and groups and can you just highlight what types of consulting work the Steele Foundation performed.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Well, first of all, it's a growing organisation. It's a very professional organisation. We have offices now in London, in New Delhi, and Mexico City, and Sao Paulo, we are hoping to open an office in Saudi Arabia. And then we have several offices throughout the United States. It's in the business of providing crisis management consulting to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. primarily corporations and in some cases to governments. We have -- we have an executive security branch, and that executive security branch protects people from -- well, let's just use the word "bodyguard," but that's not really a good word because we are much more bodyguards. In fact, we are the only private company in the world that protects the president of a nation today. We also protected the Arch Bishop of Canterbury. We just recently finished a protective detail for the former Secretary of State Madeleine Albright. So our clients that we protect are high-level people either from government or from the entertainment industry or from business. So that's another part of our business. We do behavioural sciences, if a CEO of a corporation receives an abhorrent letter and some employee says to that CEO, I'm going to kill you because you fired me, we can evaluate that letter and tell the CEO if that's really going to -- is really a danger. So behavioural sciences is one of our areas. Information security, computer security, environmental health and safety, and a rather broad, broad capability in business investigations. So we have, I don't know, five or six profit centres, and we're deployed in various places across the globe.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: General, I'd like to now turn the focus to this case in particular. And thank you -- and I know there's more in your curriculum vitae that we do have. So I don't mean any disrespect to you in connection with that, but we would like to at least move with respect to the issues before us. So if I may, sir, with respect to this case, were you asked by the Defence attorneys to review materials and to give us an opinion in connection with various issues?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you approximately tell us when that was?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: I think it was about as early as August of 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the task was that was undertaken by you as requested by the attorneys for Dr. Stakic.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Well, there's a combination of tasks, and actually when you asked me to take a look at this I guess I came up with some of my own because I thought that I needed some background information. I wanted to review material that described the creation of the federal army of Yugoslavia, and assess the missions and functions of the army and assess the relationship to the republic, to the local municipality, and to the police forces in the area. I wanted to examine the command and control system, doctrinal issues, rules of engagement, definitions of military terms, lines of responsibility of the military forces, military officers, and how they interacted, law enforcement agencies, police officers, civilian authorities at the municipal level. So those are some of the things that I took a look at.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, if you look on page 2, obviously, on Section 2, the task undertaken, in the last paragraph there you state: "It is imperative if one is going to provide an assessment and opinion on facts which transpired during April-September 1992, one must and is compelled to examine both sides of the conflict in order to avoid the presentation of a distorted, biased, prejudiced view of the events." Sir, tell us why you believe it's necessary and compelling to examine both sides of a conflict.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: In any conflict -- in a conflict there are usually two belligerents, they each have an opinion and a view and to find some balance and how that all came about and what is taking place in the particular time we are interested in, in this particular case, those dates that you suggested, one must take a look at what motivates each side.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you share with us, sir, some of the materials you reviewed in connection with formulating the opinions in creating the report that we have?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Some of the materials reviewed, and there were other items, but certainly I looked at the indictment, and that was a start point for me. I looked at Ewan Brown's report, the expert witness of the Prosecution. I looked at the testimony of Mr. Brown. I looked at Richard Butler's report, and Richard Butler, as I understand it, is a military expert that testified in another case here at the Tribunal and found his report to be very interesting. I looked at some academic and historic reports. I think Donia was one, who wrote one. Trifkovic and Gostin [phoen]. I looked at some maps and some diagrams just to get a feel for the geography and the geometry involved in the situation and in this case at hand. I looked at some videotapes, saw videotapes of activities in camps, visitations by the press to certain camps. I looked at videotapes and saw some combat situations and some exchanges of combat activity. I look at some witness transcripts, some newspaper clippings. I certainly looked at some combat reports of the VRS. I looked at military rules, regulations, and laws as it pertained to the former JNA which evolved then into the VRS, and I looked at some police reports. So there's just some of the documents, some of the categories of documents that I reviewed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry. To facilitate proceedings, it would be helpful when in the future you're making reference to reports, you may know that these reports are ongoing reports, and they are updated, that you specify the date of the report you had available. This is especially true for the Butler report and the Trifkovic report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Would the Court like me to ask him the dates of those two reports?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: When we come to this. Please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, the next section of your report, page 5, which is Section 4, "General Issues to be Addressed and Analysis and Opinion," are these the issues sir that you addressed in your report in connection with the material you reviewed and the opinions you are going to share with us?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Yes, there are eight issues that I set out and highlighted in the report. Do you want me to touch on those?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, if you don't mind.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Okay. First of all, the question of whether the military is and was susceptible to orders and directives from civilian authorities in the area where the conflict and combat was taking place was an issue that I examined. And then the military response to provocations and to attacks involving loss of life in the military forces. And then I took a look obviously at the -- regarding the May 22nd, 1992, Hambarine incident, and the justification of the military action that followed that incident. And then the May 24th Kozarac incident, and the military attack that followed that and its justification or lack thereof. And then the 30 May 1992 Prijedor attack and the military attack that followed in the city and whether it was justified or not. And then I also examined the issue of the military securing an area where an attack took place temporarily displacing civilians and personnel into camps before searching for the offenders, the rationale for all of that, and was the military justified in detaining suspects for six to eight weeks at a time. And then finally the punishment by local or military authorities of criminal actions that took place in the region in question, because it appears that there was a lot of rogue bands of thugs, some acting quasi military, that were perpetrating crimes in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your next section, sir, page 7, Section 5, it gives us a general overview of some concepts. I'd like to first address with you and have you explain to us the doctrine of the unity of command. Can you tell us what the doctrine is and how it works.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Well, I think the doctrine of the unity of command is probably as old as the military. Unity of command implies that there is one person in charge. And I think even Chuang Tzu in his book written thousands of years ago, a wonderful Chinese tactician and strategist said that unity of command is a significant principle of war. One person must be in charge. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. One person must be able to make the decision. Outside influences cannot affect that person making that decision. Certainly he can get recommendations from his staff, his military staff, because they might know something that he doesn't know. But in the end, unity of command pertains, and it's the commander that implements a decision, that offers a decision, that comes to a decision, and that takes action. So outsiders, civilian people, police authorities, politicians, they don't play in this game. They can't. Because combat is a very fast-moving situation, and you must have one person in charge so that he can take the action necessary to accomplish the mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you share with us what the doctrine chain of command implies or what it is with respect to the military.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Well, chain of command and unity of command are brothers. Unity of command implies that one person makes a decision. Chain of command implies that there is a hierarchy. And chain of command suggests that there are subordinates. So a commander, let's say a commander at the corps level, decides to take action in a particular area, creates a mission, and sends that requirement down the chain of command to his next subordinate and directs him to take action. That's the chain of command in action. That's also a unity of command in action because now that battalion commander becomes responsible for whatever that mission is, and together the battalion commander and the corps commander are fully responsible for all that happens or doesn't happen with regard to that activity. So chain of command suggests there's a hierarchy, and there's a flow of information, and there is a relationship between senior and subordinate that is clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, from your review of the materials that you highlighted for us including the military rules of the former Yugoslavia, namely the JNA as well as the army of Republika Srpska, did you find that there was a specific chain of command within the structure of those rules, regulations, and laws?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Yes, there's clearly, as one would expect, a chain of command, and there is a relationships from echelon to echelon. And clearly, there is transmission of instructions and transmission of missions, and there's a flow of information in both directions so that there's clarity and so that the people in charge can take decisions that are reasoned.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: At any point, sir, do the rules, regulations, and laws of the former Yugoslavia as well as that of within Vojska Republika Srpska, including your experience, did they ever contemplate that local civilian municipal leaders would be involved in any such chain of command?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: I never saw any evidence in the documentation that I looked at that suggested that. And it would be a peculiar circumstance where that might happen. It certainly isn't a common thing if it happens anywhere in the world, among any army in the world. I can see maybe in an extreme situation for example where there's a natural disaster and civil action is required, and huge, huge numbers of people are required to put a village or a city or restore some facility back to some sense of normalcy, where the military could be called upon by the political leaders of a municipality, of a city, of a county, and no doubt the military would respond in that situation because there would be extracurricular rules that would allow that to happen. And that's probably about the only way that it would happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, you state when you discuss unity of command what would happen --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the counsel and witness make a break between question and answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, when you discuss unity of command on page 10 of your report, you discuss what the problems would be if in fact this unity of command doctrine is breached by the infiltration of any local, civilian, municipal authorities or any local politicians for that matter. What do you mean when you say that a commander cannot serve two "bosses" and why would that be a violation and something that is impractical in terms of warfare?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: It especially applies to an ongoing combat situation where military forces are moving to contact, finding targets, and taking decisions. They can't stop as they pass through the town to ask the mayor, what is it, mayor, that you would like for us to do? And the mayor would give them instructions. It doesn't work that way. The mayor first of all isn't trained in military affairs; he's not trained in tactics; he's not trained in strategy. So this juggernaut, this military, this entity called the military, has got to control itself in outside influence. If there's more than one boss, the commander would have to make choices. Well, here's a civilian politician, a very high level, who wants me to do this, but my mission is to do that. It won't work. He can't make that choice. He has got to go and take on the mission assigned to him through the military. It's just plain as the nose on my face that there's no way that he can work for two bosses.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And now, if you can share with us what your "stove pipe" analysis model is and help us have a better understanding of that. It's reflected, for the Court and the OTP, on page 11, Section 6.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: I was trying to conjure up some idea on how I could better explain what I was talking about here, so I thought of stove pipes. Stove pipes run from the stove right through the roof and out and exhaust themselves. When you have a stove pipe, certain things go up and down in that stove pipe. You have a military stove pipe. Missions, requirements, logistical needs, operational matters, flow up and down the stove pipe. The chain of command is in that stove pipe. People are all aware within that stove pipe of what's going on. And then I thought, well there's probably a police stove pipe, a law enforcement stove pipe where the same sort of activity takes place. And they don't necessarily cross over, these two stove pipes. And then there's probably a third one called the political stove pipe, and they don't necessarily cross over with the other two. So what I was trying to do was isolate the fact that operations, administration, and maintenance takes place, missions and roles, inside these stove pipes, and there's very little crossover, and that was what I was trying to describe, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: General, you can take it that the Bench and the parties have read your report and, therefore, maybe it's appropriate to limit the comments to the so-called extras, the remarks you want to make to these parts. But please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Then the next section in your analysis, you do an analysis of the authority, the establishment of the VRS, Vojska Republika Srpska, from in fact the former JNA of Yugoslavia, and you show us what the rules and regulations are from each of the levels within the chain of command. And then you share with us also the appointment authority as well as the disciplinary authority within the military. If I can just ask you in a nutshell there, who had the authority in the military of the VRS in the spring and summer of 1992 to appoint people to certain positions? And for everyone, I think it's on page 22 of your documents.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Within the military stove pipe, the military have the authority to appoint people to certain positions. I believe in other documentation that points out that the president is responsible for appointing corps commanders, and then working down from there, there's a system within this military organisation to allow the appointment of new commanders, the changing of assignments. So inside the military stove pipe, it's military people that appoint military people to take on positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And does it not also indicate who is at the top of this chain of command, if you will, in the stove pipe analysis for the military?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: At the top of the chain of command is the president. He's a civilian. And there are some indications also that there's a Secretary of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Defence or minister of Defence who is also involved in this. Those are the two key civilians that affect the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Although perhaps clear, if I may just clarify one point, when you say the "president," it's the president of the country or the president of the republic, correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Yes, the president of the country or the republic, the federal leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's not the local municipal leader, is it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is there any indication from the military documents that you reviewed in connection with the opinions that you're going to render here today for us and as reflected in your report whether the local civilian authorities had any input as to who may be appointed to any position within the military?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: I saw absolutely no evidence that would suggest that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In fact, even in your military, sir, there's no evidence that the local politicians are involved in terms of coordinating or cooperating or appointing anyone to a certain authority level in the military. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Could counsel just clarify "your military," what's he's --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The United States military. I apologise to Mr. Koumjian.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Would you say it again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, within the documents that you reviewed namely from the former Yugoslavia that you highlighted for us as well as your experience while being in the United States military, did you find any documents which would support or even infer that a local politician would have any involvement in the command or coordination or appointment authority of military men?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: I saw no evidence of that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And sir, can you tell us or give us your opinion if that's something that's normal within the military ranks, that there would be no provision for a local politician or a local municipal leader to be involved in the military? Is that something that's excluded because of some reason or rationale?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: I think it's a normal modus operandi, because if it is not exercised that way, then you have already violated the whole principle of the chain of command and unity of command by bringing in people outside the stove pipe to tell that stove pipe how to operate.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to direct our attention to pages 24 through 26 of your report.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: All right, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And there are, sir, we talk about the discipline authorities and you highlight for us some of the rules that you reviewed as to what would occur if a subordinate or any military man would violate the rules of his military command. Who has the right, sir, to punish the individual who violated or was in derelict of his duties while serving in the military? Would it be, sir, the civilian local municipal leaders or who?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: It's the military, not the civilian local leaders. It's still inside the stove pipe, so you see we have quite a complete system.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is it true, sir, that the former Yugoslav rules and bylaws that were incorporated with the Vojska Republika Srpska, or I should say army Republika Srpska, did they also follow that disciplinary authority and chain of command as you suggested?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Yes, they did, in fact the documents suggest, strongly suggest, the evidence is there, that the doctrine of that original JNA was simply transferred over to the new organisation. And so it became a mature organisation immediately because it took on those mature doctrines, rules, regulations, ideas, and concepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: General Wilmot, help me understand, if a military man is on leave from his military duties and including your stove pipe analysis, but the military man commits a violation of the law or in essence a crime, who would, under your stove pipe analysis, be required to investigate and punish that individual?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: The military would.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And why so, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Because the person is a member of the military organisation, recognised as such, and comes under the rules and regulations of the military and how it deports itself in public. So while I can see an instance where possibly a civilian authority might arrest a military person on the street, the military would end up with that person and would be the ones that would indict, investigate, indict, and possibly punish if found guilty.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, when you say "civilian authority," to whom are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: I could be referring to the police that might arrest this person or the police -- or even a political organisation possibly that somehow reports to the police that this person is doing something in public that is contrary to the rules, please arrest them. So that's -- I'm talking about the entire civilian population, no matter what their duties, responsibilities may be.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In your stove pipe analysis, sir, and from the police documents as well as the military documents that you reviewed, is the police structure, although referred to as a civilian structure, is it separate and distinct from the civilian political leadership?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Yes, my research certainly suggests that it is very much a separate entity, and it represents also a stove pipe.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that stove pipe, sir, I think from what's reflected at least in your report and from some of the testimony you reviewed goes from the initial police officers, the reserve police officers, the regular police officers, through the chief of the stations and all the way to the Minister of Interior Affairs which is referred to as here as I think MUP, M-U-P. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, do you have an opinion, sir, based upon a reasonable degree of sent as to whether the rules and regulations and laws of the military concerning the former Yugoslavia, namely the JNA and the VRS, were they sophisticated rules and regulations? Did you find them to be?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Yeah, I found them to be a very mature and very sophisticated. They were clear, they were instructive, they were easily understood, and certainly they could be followed without any difficulty. But yes, they were mature and sophisticated.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, let's move to the events specifically leading up to the conflict in the Prijedor municipality in the spring and summer of 1992. From your review of the articles, the military reports, the police reports, among other things, did you examine what events led up to the actions that took place in May of 1992 in the municipality of Prijedor, and if so, did you find any of them to be significant?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Yes, I did examine the events, and I made a quick overview in my report of those events. It was primarily to put in context the situation so that I could understand it more clearly, but there was a lot of activity, there were skirmishes, there were people being shot at, there were attacks. There were armies being formed. There were republics being formed. There was mobilisation taking place, and there was great stress and great strain among the population as to -- and fearfulness as to what was going to transpire and what was going to happen. So it was a time of chaos and confusion, and it was simply a time where one knew that combat was probably going to follow, but didn't know in what form. So there was fearfulness in the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, were there attacks from your review on the JNA military at any point during the period of 1992 that you reviewed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What is the significance of that, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: There seemed to be a fleeing of some people from the JNA identified I guess as Muslims primarily. And then attacks on the JNA as Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. it tried to leave its barracks or as it travelled down a road moving some of its supplies, equipment, and vehicles. And so there seemed to be a situation going on where contending forces were being set up and developed. And now we had belligerents facing each other, and those belligerants took action against each other. For example, I think it was on May the 3rd, a JNA column out of Sarajevo was ambushed and attacked by Muslim units. And a military column on the 15th of May, leaving Tuzla, was attacked by Muslim units, and there was quite a few casualties there, something like I guess somewhere between 170 and 200 were killed, and 150 wounded and 300 were taken prisoner. Now, that's a significant combat event.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Immediately prior to that event, if we can have the Madam Registrar show the General Exhibit D6. And, sir, while they are presenting that to you, it's a dispatch that was issued with respect to an instruction to attack or to prevent military convoys from leaving Bosnia and Herzegovina territory. And is that one of the documents that you reviewed and referred to in your report, specifically pages 32 and 33.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, this was according to some of the testimony intercepted by the Serbs in the Prijedor Municipality, and there's some indication, at least from the representations made by the Office of the Prosecution, that that was withdrawn or that was considered to be a falsified report that was issued. Your opinion, sir, based upon a reasonable degree of certainty, in light of this April 29th, 1992, dispatch, and the two events that you just highlighted to us, namely May 3rd and May 13th, 1992, where there were attacks on convoys, do you have an opinion as to whether or not these orders are actually followed and convoys were stopped in the area of the former Yugoslavia and attacks were made upon the JNA?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: There's a relationship between this message and what transpired, so I would assume -- I would have to assume that they were carrying out these orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, you discussed the May 3rd event where approximately seven JNA soldiers were ambushed and killed. Can you tell us which documentation you relied on in order to form that conclusion. I think it's footnote 70, if I'm not mistaken, to move it along.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: It's an academic report, historian report, in fact there was a General McKenzie newspaper and there was a newspaper column. General McKenzie in the process of writing a book, and I believe it's been published, mentioned this event. So it's from his document

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In fact, sir, it's a war diary that General McKenzie maintained and --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: -- kept contemporaneous with the events as they unfolded on or about May 3rd, 1992. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Objection, leading the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In the interests of time, I was, but I can restate the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you look in the binders there and pull out for us, to the extent that you have it, footnote 70. Thank you. Can you tell us, sir, while you're looking and to the extent you found it what do you have as your footnote number 70?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: It's General McKenzie, Lewis McKenzie's United Nations Protection Force, a convoy incident, and it's from a diary that he wrote. And that's where I found this material.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, directing you to the third page of that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry, may I interrupt here. You state: "Relied upon various accounts presented by academic historians." So your testimony would be in footnote 70, you relied on Mr. McKenzie's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, General McKenzie's account.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So not plural, but single. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the witness is referring to a document, I think it's appropriate that we get an opportunity to see the document the witness is referring to. We don't have a copy of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: General, if you don't mind, if you open the binder, you can then take out the document and we can perhaps place it on the ELMO. Or then the usher can assist you in doing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: During the break, copies can be provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The usher will assist you, General. Would the usher be kind enough to put footnote 70 on the ELMO for us, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: General, on the screen before you, you should have a reflection of what's placed on the ELMO. Is that the report, sir, that you reviewed or at least a part of it from General -- Major-General Lewis McKenzie's report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Book, I should say. And below immediately it shows the convoy incident May 3rd, correct, 1992?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I apologise for leading, but can we turn to page 3 of that report, sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, is this going into evidence? Then we will have to describe what else is on the page. If it isn't then I'd like to describe --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We would like it to. I don't know if it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If you tender this, we shouldn't go in formal details, only that we ensure that we have it, and only that we know what's underlying footnote 70. Do I take it correctly that also footnote 71 is based on the same source?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: There's another footnote, and we'll get to that if I may, Your Honour. It's an article as well as --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's a news article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay, then may I ask Madam Registrar what would be the next D number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D95, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, of course, I reserve my right to object having not seen the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We proceed as usual. It's provisionally marked D95, and then later on, we ask for objections, if any. So please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, on page 3 of that document, is it reflected on the second to the last paragraph from the bottom the incident involved that's reflected in your report where seven JNA military men were killed? Can you read that section to us, please.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: "Some 200 JNA soldiers had disappeared. At first I assumed they had bolted for the Serb-controlled area just south of the ambush site. Later I had discovered that they had been taken prisoner. All of the JNA weapons and military equipment of any value was confiscated by the TDF, and six to seven JNA officers had been killed in cold blood. During the incident, our modest UN presence of ten people had prevented a massive blood bath."

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, if I can ask you to turn to page 1 of that document so that the TDF can be defined for us on this incident of May 3rd, 1992, and I think immediately below General McKenzie's picture.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What is the TDF as referred to by General McKenzie as it existed on May 3rd, 1992.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: He's talking about an entity called the Territorial Defence force.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is that a Serbian or Croatian Territorial Defence force, or does he state that it was a Bosnian (Muslim) TDF? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Bosnian Muslim TDF, Territorial Defence force. And he goes on to say, "who are rapidly getting out of control."

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: As a military man, what effect would the attack on a convoy and the killing of seven of your soldiers be in cold blood, what effect would that have in the region or in the territory once that news has transpired to other members of the military?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: First of all, it would probably be a very sobering piece of news. Secondly, it would put everyone on a higher alert, personal alert. And third of all, it would probably put into the mind of the ordinary soldier the idea, well, we must respond and how are we going to respond. And then among the officers, it would probably set them to thinking about a response and how to handle the situation. So I think there would be a sort of a solidarity, a resolve would develop among those who were affected.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Would tensions be on the rise?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Oh yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Would there be a higher status of alert?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely, personally and unitwise, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The next event, sir, that you have with respect to the events that may have triggered subsequent events in the Prijedor Municipality is an event that occurred, I believe, in your report it says May 15th, 1992, and you cite footnote number 71. Can you please or would the usher could be kind enough to place that on the ELMO. And while he's doing that, General, could you tell us what occurred on or about May 13th, 1992? 15th is in your report, but I think we've established that it's the 13th, correct, General, based on the article and based on what you shared with me yesterday. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, can I direct your attention, this is a newspaper article as reflected on the ELMO from -- dated May 13th, 1996. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And it's a report with respect to the anniversary of the events that happened four years prior. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And it discusses, does it not, sir, in the third paragraph the isn't that you refer to in your report, namely the attack on the Bosnian Serb army showing soldiers being killed, some being wounded, and other captured. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: That's correct, some 172 JNA soldiers were killed. Some burned to death in Tuzla, which is a town in northeastern Bosnia while more than 100 were wounded and about 140 were captured.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The article also proceeds to highlight the fact that on May 3rd, that what we just discussed, six JNA soldiers were killed in Sarajevo which is the incident you referred to earlier as reflected in General Lewis McKenzie's diaries. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Yes, same one.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What effect did that event in conjunction with the events of May 3rd, 1992, have on the military in connection with the tensions and anxieties that maybe built up on or around the area of Bosnia in 1992?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Well, I can imagine that it certainly added to the chaos, confusion, the tension, and the stress of all concerned in the area. And I can imagine that battle lines were being drawn, and people were choosing up sides, and people wanted reaction to this and wanted a response to this. And so I would anticipate that plans were being drawn up to respond to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And the two warring factions at that time essentially were the Bosnian Muslims and the Bosnian Serbs. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And at that time, were there declarations of state of imminent war?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: There were.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We're overlapping again. My fault. I apologise. Let me just restate the question because I'm not sure if the answer was provided. Were there, sir, declarations of war or state of imminent war at that time that were declared by both or either's party?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What effect from a military standpoint does that declaration have, sir, on the military personnel as well as on the general populous?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Well, it certainly increases the level of readiness. It certainly increases the level of activity. For example, if the military had not been issued ammunition for their weapons, I'm sure that by now they would have been. If the military had not formed themselves up into positions from which they could launch attacks or defend, I'm certain that this sort of activity would cause that to happen. And I'm speaking generally here. I can't tell you that they formed a defensive position around area A or area B in this particular situation we're talking about. I'm simply talking in generalities. And what I really mean to say is they're increasing they're level of readiness, they're getting ready to do something.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What effect would it have on the civilians, sir, to learn the information that the JNA soldiers were, as described by General Lewis McKenzie, "killed in cold blood" and as described in the newspaper account, that over 170 were killed? What effect would it have on civilians?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Well, that certainly is a significant number, and so I'm -- I would presume that the civilians would wonder about the security situation in the country and their own personal security, the security of their families, their children, their property. Because that was a major, major activity. And so they would wonder about what is the status, what is really going on here, and who's next?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'd like to now move to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Before we move to another document, this Tanjug news report, May 13th, 1996, would be provisionally marked D96. And in order not to make any mistake, I have to ask you, General, when you refer in footnote 71, you "relied on various accounts presented by academic historians," the underlying source would be this Tanjug news report? And what brings you to the comment "relies upon various accounts presented by academic historians"?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sorry, but the witness shook his head and the transcript didn't get his positive response to Your Honour's last question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, are you telling me that the statement 71 or the footnote 71 "relied upon various accounts presented by academic historians" which actually is a newspaper article. So it's an erroneous statement in the footnote. It's actually a newspaper article. You're telling me that that should be changed, and I should agree to it. Is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It was a question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. I think I was given something on the order of 30 hours to try to prepare this report, and it didn't turn out to be a 30-hour task. It turned out to be more like a couple hundred hours. So I think that there are probably discrepancies in the report simply because I moved along as quickly as I could. So I apologise if this in fact is not a historian report; it is in fact a news report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to now turn to the next section of your report, and that is Section 34, and to discuss the issues of confrontation, provocation, and attack, specifically as it relates to the Prijedor Municipality in the spring and summer of 1992. First, my question to you, sir, is: What is a confrontation, provocation, and attack? Page 34, not Section 34.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Well, a provocation could be a situation where some children put out rubber tyres across a road and set them on fire, and a group of people Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. or a convoy come up to that roadblock, and the children, youngsters, teenagers throw rocks at the convoy. That could be a provocation. The result of that could be a confrontation where the man in charge of the convoy goes out and tells those teenagers to get out of the way and get those tyres out of there, we're going to come through there. If the teenagers don't do that, then they might run them off and simply move the tyres and go on through. So the action taken, as you can see from my description, is quite limited and quite reasonable, get off the road, move the tyres, we're coming through. Whereas an attack might be where a convoy comes up to a roadblock and all of a sudden is under live fire and maybe someone is killed. Now, the confrontation that follows the attack might be completely different. There's an escalation factor here. The convoy commander might decide to deploy some people out of his convoy and go after the perpetrators of the attack. And that might then lead to an escalated combat situation in that area. So that's kind of the difference between the ideas of a provocation, and then a confrontation, an attack and a confrontation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Describe for us, if you will, what the rules of engagement would be when there's a provocation. And I believe for the Court, it's page 35 of the General's report.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: In a provocation, the rules of engagement should allow for an escalation where you might start out by, for example, in a rioting crowd, just breaking up the crowd, finding the leaders, arresting them, and moving them out, or arresting certain groups from that crowd and reducing their numbers and therefore dissipating their power, at least their perceived power. But anyway, you want to apply a remedy at the same level as the provocation. You don't want to kill anybody, you don't want to kill any civilian, you don't want to kill anybody, you simply want to quell this riot. That's one situation. Whereas if you come into a situation where you are under attack, and people are firing at you and people are killing -- some opponent out there, some belligerent out there is killing your troops or your people, then you have to take a more powerful reaction. And that might very well be deploying your troops and going after the attackers and clearing the -- let's say it's a roadblock in this case, and passing through, and then going into adjacent areas to find the people that created this attack, that started this attack, and to capture them, to arrest them, to interrogate them. So the rules of engagement allow you to defend yourself, and you defend yourself at the same level you were attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And these, sir, rules of engagement apply to all the militaries across the world. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Yes, I would say as a generality, that's the -- they apply everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure if they should take a break at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The trial stays adjourned until 11.00 sharp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. The usher is apparently already on his way. We use the time, Prosecution, any objections against D95, D96?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence, D95A and D96A. I take it that the Defence takes care that also Dr. Stakic understands these documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honours, the interpreters and court reporters kindly ask both speakers to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You heard --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm heard. I'm admonished to slow down, so I will do my very best to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: General, we're now going to examine the actual incidents that occurred in the Prijedor Municipality as reflected in your report, page 38, Section 9. And in fact, sir, there were approximately how many incidents that occurred over what period of time in the spring and summer of 1992 in the Prijedor Municipality from your review of the documents?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: There were three incidents, May 22nd, May 24th, and May 30th, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I apologise for rushing through some of this, sir, but it is somewhat covered in your report, and I'd like to get some exhibits in as well. Can you just generally describe for us the incident that occurred on May 22nd, 1992, at Hambarine.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: At Hambarine, there was a group of military men returning from training to their homes apparently. They came up to a checkpoint, and they were taken under attack. And two people lost their lives, from what I was able to glean from the documentation. And then there was a response, which involved requesting that those people who were responsible for the attacks be turned over to the authorities, and that everyone turn in their weapons. That didn't happen, and so there was a military response later on at the point of the attack and in the area around the attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just so that we're clear, help me understand, General, the military men that were coming back or returning to go home during their leave, were they men from the JNA, essentially Serbian combatants or Serbian military men?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And they came under attack and under fire by whom?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Apparently by a group of Muslim individuals who were manning this checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: From your review, sir, of the documents and from your experience, the military issued an ultimatum to the people within that checkpoint. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: They did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And sir, is that something that's reasonable and acceptable from a military standpoint? Do you have an opinion based upon that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Yes, I think it would be a very, very reasonable response from the military authorities in the area to ask that the perpetrators be turned over.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And once -- from your review, is that also a prudent request, a prudent initial move by the military who lost the lives of some of its personnel at that checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Very prudent indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And subsequent to that, what if anything occurred, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: The perpetrators were not turned over. Weapons were not turned in. And so the military went into the area in search of the perpetrators, and the result was that there was gunfire, exchange of fire, and a combat situation developed in and around the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you have an opinion, sir, based upon a reasonable degree of certainty based upon your education and experience as well as your review of the documents --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, my apologies.
