utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you have an upon based upon a reasonable degree of certainty, based upon your experience and education as well as from your review of the documents in connection with this case whether or not the military was justified in responding to the attack on its two personnel on May 22nd, 1992?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: In my opinion, they were fully justified in the actions that they took.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, let's turn to the next confrontation or provocation that occurred, and that would be two days later, on May 24th, 1992, at the checkpoint in Jakupovici, namely on or around the village of Kozarac. Can Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you tell us, sir, factually the backdrop from the materials that you reviewed what occurred at or about that checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Apparently, the military was in a convoy moving along the road, and they came up against a roadblock. Apparently they stopped, they were attacked. They were taken under fire, and one of their men was killed. The military responded. I assume that that means that they deployed into the areas around where the attack took place, and a combat situation developed in the immediate and the extended area.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And sir, based upon a reasonable degree of certainty, based upon your experience and education, and from the materials that you reviewed, do you have an opinion as to whether or not the military was justified to respond to the attack on its military convoy resulting in the death of its military personnel?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that they were justified in that response.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: At that point, sir, from your review of the materials, is it true that actually the -- as you call it in your report, the "enemy," they were starting a procedure of capturing them. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you describe for me under what provision does the military have or the right to capture its "enemy" at a time of engaged warfare?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: In the course of combat, if one force has overwhelming fire power and the other force sees and observes that and are willing to give themselves over as captives, then the attacking force or the more powerful force should honour that and take what I will call at this point prisoners of war, take them into detention, hold them, maybe even interrogate them at the point of capture to gather any combat intelligence that they can gather at that moment to lead them to further activity, to find further forces, other forces, that they can either destroy or capture as they move along in this process. So it is typical that in combat, if the opportunity presents itself, that one would take prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And, sir, that's also covered within the Geneva Convention as reflected --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Ultimately I'll get it done before this case is over. Thank you. Sir, and its reflected in your report that in fact the Geneva Convention, specifically Article 25 among others, covers the fact that during combat activities when you capture the detainee he is considered the prisoner of war, and they use the term "camp," do they not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Yes, they do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And can you tell us, although we'll get into the detention centres a little later or the camps as they are referred to a little later, in this circumstance, there's an issue or a term used in the military called pursuit during combat activity. Are you familiar with that term?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you describe that term to us, please.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Pursuit would involve following, chasing, attempting to corner or pin down an enemy element, and maybe the basic reason for the pursuit would be to capture them, among other things, or it may be to destroy them. But the idea is that you are in pursuit, you are chasing someone who needs to be in your view, as the attacking force, tracked down and captured. The word "camp" is used in the Geneva Convention because you can set up a very temporary camp right there behind the front lines. I call it a prisoner of war cage. It doesn't sound as nice as camp, but actually it's just a very temporary holding area where a quick interrogation is completed. And then the doctrine for every army that I know of is to take that prisoner, that person that you captured after pursuit, and take them to the rear area into a more permanently established camp where they can be interrogated again and detained, taken off the battlefield, nullified as a threat to the force that captured them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Which entity, sir, considering and in light of your stove pipe analysis, would be the one that would discharge the duties to arrest, capture, interrogate, and detain members of the opposing army or opposing forces?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: It would be the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me now with the Court's permission ask the usher to show you the rules, some of which you reviewed from the federal secretariat for national defence, caption military secret, ERN number 03030230. If I can direct the usher, it's on the stack of documents underneath some of those books. I could perhaps help you, to speed things up in light of the time. Thank you. And perhaps with the Court's permission, he can place it on the ELMO, first the cover sheet, and then I would say ask you turn to page 119.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You don't have copies for the parties or is it 65 terred already?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We are in the process of making them, Your Honour. We will get that to the Court. We thought we had made copies, and apparently we stand corrected on that. So my apologies to the Court and to counsel. But I believe they have it because it's their 65 ter number. It's a document we received from them at some point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We'll come back to this later. Provisionally marked D97.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Once again, I stand corrected. It is 65 terred, number 562.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: As we can see on the ELMO, this is the cover page of the federal secretariat for national defence, caption military secret internal, brigade rules, et cetera, 1994. Sir, I'd ask that the usher please show you page 119 of that document and place it on the ELMO. Specifically, sir, examining Section 13, with respect to pursuit in combat activities, can you please read for us Section 13, subsection 455 and 456.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: "Pursuit is a combat tactical activity which is the result of a successful attack. The goal of pursuit is to develop existing results, prevent the enemy from pulling out of combat and retreating in order to get organised once again, in accordance with his plans for combat, and then to rout, surround, and destroy the enemy." "456: The brigade will successfully pursue the enemy by constantly reconnoitring, monitoring, and identifying the enemy actions and intentions, maintaining constant combat contact, prompt commencement of pursuit, coordinated action of the forward, and pursuit detachments and pursuit columns with the TO units and forces in the enemy rear, pursuing the enemy on a wide front, maintaining a compact pursuit disposition, and ridding the units of unnecessary gear."

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That would be adequate for now. Can you just tell us what it means under subsection 456, "pursuing the enemy on a wide front."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Let's say there is a point of attack, there is a point of contact, the enemy retreats from that point of contact, let's say we are calling ourselves the friendly force in this case. We as the friendly force deploy and possibly we are a battalion-size unit, and we deploy our entire battalion across a wide front, like maybe 800, 900, 1200 metres wide, and conduct a pursuit, a sweeping action through the area, looking for those forces that conducted the attack at the point we started from. So wide pursuit includes deployment of your unit, covering much more ground than you were covering at the point of attack in search of the people that are attempting to retreat, escape, and fight another day.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, with respect to May 24th, 1992, there was certainly a pursuit of the enemy on a wide front as you have described. Was the military justified in accordance with both your experience and your knowledge and education as well as that from the Yugoslav military documents to continue this pursuit in a wide front?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let's just briefly -- we'll come back to May 24th with respect to the detention centres later in the section captioned detention centres or camps. Let's just move next to the next date in which there was an attack by the Bosnian Muslims, and that would have been how many days after May 24th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Six days, May 30th, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is that significant, sir, that within ten days, there were three attacks on the military and in the town of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: It is significant. It sounds like war, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, what effect, if any, would three specific attacks within a ten-day period have on both the military personnel and their commanders on or around the area of the Prijedor Municipality?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: They would certainly be tightening up their security operations. They would certainly be considering plans. They would certainly be considering reconnaissance activities, and they would certainly be considering intelligence and intelligence estimates and other threats that might come to fruition in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Share with us the backdrop that you reviewed from the materials provided to you in connection with the May 30th, 1992, attack and incident that occurred in the city/town of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Well, apparently Muslim forces come across the river, and I think it's the Sava River, into the town of Prijedor and took it under attack, attacking various facilities in the city, and this fighting went on for several hours. And apparently the military force there and the police forces there were both taken by surprise, and so initially, the attacking force had the advantage. And it took quite a while to drive them out of the city and back across the river.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And it's the Sana River, as opposed to the Sava River.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Sana, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Help me with this: Also the military at this point, did they continue to pursue or were they in pursuit of the "enemy" as a result of the May 30th, 1992, attack upon the city/town of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Yes, they did pursue the attacking forces, but they also stopped in I guess I would describe it as a suburb neighbourhood. I've never been there so I don't know exactly how to describe it called Stari Grad, is it? And they decimated that neighbourhood, which is contrary to the rules of land warfare and probably criminal action if one would take a look at it and if certain -- and if authorities would examine what happened there, it was an atrocity, and something that the army should have been brought to account on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let's break down the events as they related to May 30th, 1992. The initial attack by the Bosnian Muslim forces in the city/town and the response by the military, was that response, sir, justified based upon a reasonable degree of certainty and based upon your review of the materials in conjunction with your experience and education?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: The response of driving out the attacking force was certainly justified. The actions in that small ethnic neighbourhood were not justified.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We'll get to that in a second. After the military started pursuing the forces outside the city/town of Prijedor and into Stari Grad, do you have an opinion as to whether or not the military action taken on or around Stari Grad by virtue of the pursuit by the military on May 30th, 1992, was justified?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: It was justified.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And what you're saying, sir, in addition to that is that the attack that led to the actual Stari Grad after the pursuit and the essential destruction of the entire Stari Grad, was that, sir, justified in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And why not, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Because the forces went into a built-up, civilian area, and it appears to me as if they simply vented their hatred, destroying homes, destroying businesses probably, the livelihood of those people that lived in that neighbourhood, and that's contrary to all the rules of land warfare.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Who, sir, in your opinion, is responsible and authorised to file a complaint against the military as a result of the action that was taken on the village of Stari Grad on May 30th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Can you ask the question again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sure, my apologies. As a result of the action that was taken that you opine is unjustified in the village of Stari Grad, does the military command structure allow for the military to report that activity and ultimately to punish or start proceedings to investigate and to punish the perpetrators of the attack on Stari Grad on May 30th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Yes, the command structure does allow for that, and it should have been occurred. But it's broader than that. Anyone in the military could have reported this event and this criminal action, and as a result of that report, it should have been investigated, it should have been evaluated, and then people brought to task who were leading the effort. So even the foot soldier could have reported such an incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Only that the transcript is correct, did you say "anyone in the military could have reported" or "should have reported"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I thought the question was structured in such a way that the answer would be could have. The answer also could be should have, because every soldier is obligated to report a criminal or a law that's a -- a command that is illegal. In the case of Lieutenant Kelly in Vietnam --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's stay here in the area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Because this would be based on the manual in A, providing the obligation to report. Right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In any of those -- strike that. Sir, now let's focus quickly, if we may, on the detention camps specifically page 45 of the General's report, and the issues surrounding that. There were three detention centres in the Prijedor Municipality in essence in and around the spring of 1992. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I know you advised me the names are somewhat difficult to pronounce.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Trnopolje was one of them I believe, close to the pronunciation. And let me see if I can find the other two.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me just help you in the interests of time. Keraterm and Omarska were the other two, correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Yes, Keraterm and Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And these detention camps as you've mentioned, pursuant to Article 25 of the Geneva Convention, are they, sir, authorised to be set up?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Yes, it's good form for the military to establish camps to the rear. Those camps, therefore, offer protection to combatants who are now disarmed and are no longer in the conflict. Those camps should also provide medical facilities, food, housing comparable and similar to what the troops in the field are using, and so yes, they are authorised to set them up, and it's good form to set them up.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, let me ask you, these camps were set up as a result of what?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: These camps were set up as a result of the number of prisoners that were being taken, the number of detainees that were being taken, and the confusion in the area where the conflict was being conducted. And so what the military force did in this case was simply begin to extract large numbers of people and move them to I'll describe it as move them to the rear so that they could sort out who was who. Detain them, question them, find out who they were, and what role they played in that particular area, and get them away from the combat zone so that the real enemy could be contended with.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, help me understand the process, in detaining individuals who were suspects during a battle, namely three specific battles against the military within ten days, is there a procedure that is utilised during the interrogation process. For example, would you, once you interrogate detainee number 1, immediately release detainee number 1, and if not, why not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: No, you wouldn't release detainee number 1, you would hold detainee number 1 until you've interrogated everybody that's waiting in line. So it's a lengthy process, it takes time, because you may find that detainee number 392 has something significant to say about detainee number 1. And if you had let him go, you may have just let go a commander of one of the opposing forces without even knowing it. So it's a long process, it requires holding people over time so that you are able to build an understanding of who everybody is that was picked up that was detained that is now being held.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With the Court's permission, I'd like to have the usher place provisions of the Geneva Convention on the ELMO, specifically Section 2, Article 118. It starts on the bottom of that page and proceeds to the next page. Sir, I'd like to ask you this question while we're looking at this provision of the Geneva Convention. Can you tell me, based upon a reasonable degree of certainty your experience and education how long detainees are required to be kept in detention camps as a general premise?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Detainees can be kept in detention for the duration of the hostilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can we --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Civilian detainees, I think generally speaking, 90 days unless something is discovered in their background that would cause you to keep them longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let's examine what it says specifically on Article 118. It starts under Section 2, and if you could read the entire section for us, and then I think it proceeds on the next page concluding.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: "Prisoners of war shall be released and repatriated without delay after the cessation of hostilities."

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Of active hostilities. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to get it clear on the record. Who decides when the active hostilities cease, and in this case, when did the active hostilities cease in the former Yugoslavia, specifically in the Prijedor Municipality?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Normally, there is a -- some sort of a peace process that takes place. And the contending parties agree to certain terms for that peace process to be finalised, and at some point, you have a cessation of hostilities agreed to by all parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And the Geneva Convention, sir, does not specify what the time frame is for the release of these detainees other than to say "upon cessation of active hostilities." Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: As far as I know, that's the only -- that's the only terms of releasing prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, these prisoners of war detainees are being held in a detention camp as allowed by the Geneva Convention, and they are being interrogated to determine what, the criminal proceedings that may be brought against them?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: They are being interrogated for the intelligence and the information that they may be able to offer about activities that are taking place in the field. They're being interrogated about their relationship to enemy elements in the field. They are being interrogated as to what their status really is in society so that they can be identified as noncombatants who have no impact on the situation, prisoners of war, or possibly even criminals.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And sir, let me now direct your attention quickly if I may to the Yugoslav orders and rule on the application of the international law of war in the armed forces of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia which is Defence 65 ter number 561. If the usher would be kind to first show us the front page, and just for the record has ERN number 00807690. And we'll be looking specifically at Section 240 which has the ERN number 00807754.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This would be provisionally marked D97, but we have to come back to this because of the poor quality of the copies we have received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D98, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If we may just turn to the applicable section, I believe to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I have to correct myself. As normal, Madam Registrar is correct. The previous 65 ter 562 that was D97, and what we now have before us, 65 ter number 561, this indeed would be D98. Thank you for this assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, General --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may proceed, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: General, examining the rules or orders in the Yugoslav military as it existed at that time, they also had a provision, did they not, sir, with respect to detaining forces that were enemy to the actual army?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sorry. General, we must keep all our answers verbal, and no nods of the head or shrugs of the shoulders because our court reporters cannot take down such shrugs or nods, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, with respect to the conflicts that were arising in the Prijedor Municipality in the spring and summer of 1992, based upon the review of the military documents that existed from the former JNA and from the VRS, the army of Republika Srpska, was the military justified in capturing -- after these three incidents capturing suspects and detaining them in what was called as camps?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, sir, based upon the provisions, specifically the provision that's before you, I believe provision 240, was there a law that existed that allowed the military to detain these individuals who were captured and placed in these camps for a certain number of period -- or for a certain period of time before they either proceed with criminal proceedings or they released them? Was there a specific time frame set out in the rules of the Yugoslav military regulations and laws?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And we're kind of ahead of ourselves but we pointed that out on paragraph 240 of this section of the rules. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you read to us, sir, that section so we have it in the record and tell us specifically what the time frame is that the military is authorised to detain people who are suspects during essentially warfare.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Article 240, criminal Prosecution: "No prisoner of war may be tried or punished for an act not explicitly specified by the laws of the detaining power, or by international law, in force when the act was committed. Immediately upon capture, prisoners of war should be informed of the criminal acts entailing capital punishment. After their being so informed, capital punishment may not be pronounced on a prisoner of war for any other criminal offence without the consent of the power on which he depends. Criminal proceedings must be conducted as quickly as possible. Custody may not last longer than three months. The time spent in custody shall be included in the serving of a prison sentence."

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, in the present situation, namely the Prijedor Municipality, as a result of those three incidents in May of 1992 and the arrest and detention of prisoners of war or what they believed were the "enemy" at that time, the Yugoslav rules allowed that these detainees be kept in detention camps for 90 days, three months. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Or criminal prosecution should begin, and if it doesn't begin, they should be released. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sometime in August, whether it's August 5th or August 6th, 1992, the Keraterm and Omarska camps were closed. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And now these camps were commenced to operate immediately after May 24th, 1992, namely the attack on Kozarac. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is that, sir, based upon your opinion - I'm asked to slow down, I apologise. Is that, sir, based upon your opinion a reasonable amount of time to keep detainees in so-called camps, from May 24th through let's even say the mid of August 1992?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The hostilities in former Bosnia and Herzegovina, in the former Yugoslavia, ceased sometime in 1995 as we discussed before. If they kept these detainees for a longer period beyond that point based upon the Geneva Conventions, were they permitted to do so?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: From your review of the material, sir, can you tell us who administered, maintained, and operated the detention centres in or around the Prijedor Municipality in the spring and summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: They were operated by the military, and there was some assistance from the local law enforcement authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That would be the police. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Police, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'd like to just skip ahead a little bit, and I apologise if we're running short on time, and have you look at what we've identified as Defence 65 ter number 316, 317, and 318. This involves, just so that we could speed the process, the issues of Mount Vlasic where 150 or so Bosnian Muslims were killed. And I'd like to show these documents to the General, with the usher's assistance and the Court's permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: At the moment, admittedly also after a long search and seizure attempt, we didn't find these 65 ter numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If you have additional copies, it would be good. Otherwise, it should be put on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We will place it on the ELMO, Your Honour. I was unfortunately under the misimpression that the complete set was provided to the Court and to our learned friends at the Office of the Prosecution. Again, our apologies for that. We hope to get it no later than today, 3.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If we can just move or scan back a little so we can get the entirety of the document reflected on the ELMO. This, General, has the -- now I can't see the ERN number, but for the record it has the ERN number 00635446. It's a document dated September 11th, 1992, on the top, and it seems to have two or three other signators within the document. Sir, this document, in essence, is a request by the police in the stove pipe analysis that you utilised from Banja Luka directing the -- the minister of interior --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: At the same time so that we don't lose the order, this would be provisionally marked D98.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: 99, I believe, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You are really too fast, not only in speaking but also in providing documents. D99.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, this involved the tragic incident from Mount Vlasic. Is there -- in this case, there's an allegation as you've read in the indictment that there was nothing to prevent or punish individuals. Does this document, sir, request that the police chief in the Prijedor Municipality start an investigation and conduct or issue any charges against the individuals involved in the Mount Vlasic attack?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And can we turn with the usher's kind assistance to the next page, and that would be I believe the response to this letter from the police chief himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: D100, provisionally marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just for the record, this is dated the 14th of September, 1992, and the previous one, I believe, is the 14th -- or the 11th. I'm mistaken.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The previous document was dated 14th September, and the record says 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: This is a response to that letter, correct, that was issued requesting that there be an investigation. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, we can all read it. It's on the ELMO. The first paragraph essentially is a response saying that the individuals who were involved in the convoy are -- have been deployed to another area and are serving duty. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What interests me most, General, is the second paragraph. Who, sir, based upon that second paragraph from this exhibit does it reflect was actually taking the convoy and who was in charge of as it states "providing physical security for the convoy" and who required the individuals to do so?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: The army and the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Anywhere, sir, does it show that the civilian municipal authorities, namely the political leaders within the Prijedor Municipality, requested or sought that the police provide security for the convoys that resulted on the 21st of August, 1992, massacre at Mount Vlasic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: No, it does not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is there any evidence, sir, in the documents that you reviewed which would suggest, infer, or establish that the civilian municipal authorities at any time had any command or authority over the police or military involving any incidents relating to the Mount Vlasic massacre on August 21st, 1992?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can we turn to the next letter that was written in connection with this issue. I believe that's a letter dated the 13th of October, 1992, which has the ERN number -- it's under our 65 ter number -- the ERN number actually is 00633338 in the B/C/S version, but they did not incorporate another ERN number on the English version. So that's why the English version does not have an ERN number. Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I can't see any date on the screen here.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: On the top left-hand corner, the third line, Your Honour. I stand corrected, Your Honour. I'm looking at a different document. The document on the ELMO, correct, does not have a date.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is another letter by the police chief Simo Drljaca from the Prijedor Municipality in connection with a request to identify the individuals who were at Mount Vlasic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Does that letter, sir, in fact state that a list was provided of those individuals and they give a Document Number and the date of the letter which identified those individuals involved in the Mount Vlasic massacre?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Would you restate the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sure. Does the letter that we're looking at --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: -- does that letter, sir, reflect that Simo Drljaca, the police chief of the Prijedor police station, public security station, that he sent information that was requested about the policemen who had escorted the convoy on the 21st of August, 1992?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: He said that he sent information on the policemen, active and reserve, on August 21st, 1992. Yes, he did say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Who escorted the convoy. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Who escorted the convoy, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: At that point, sir, assuming that it was given or even assuming that it was not, do the civilian authorities in the municipality of Prijedor have any involvement whatsoever in the pursuit of the criminals who perpetrated these acts at Mount Vlasic among other places in the spring and summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: No, they don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This document would be D101 provisionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe this may be already marked as S275, if the Registrar could just double check that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'd like now to generally ask you a couple questions about some of the other binders that you put together for us. In a general sense, sir, from the documents that you reviewed, can you describe for us whether the chaos and the tensions were always at an all-time high in the Prijedor Municipality during the spring and summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: No. There was a period of time in the early spring when things were quite calm in Prijedor. And in fact, the Serbs, the Serb faction, claimed Prijedor as their own, and they did it without firing a shot, without interrupting any commercial activity, without interrupting anyone's lives. And it seemed as if everyone agreed with that status. Things were calm. People were getting along. And activities were normal, and everything was relatively quiet.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you have an opinion, sir, since that point when the Serb takeover, namely April 30th, 1992, up until what point was everything relatively quiet?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Everything was relatively quiet up until the point of the checkpoint incident, and then that was the first of the three incidents that seemed to ignite tension, stress, and chaos, and confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may just show you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt for a moment that we don't have to come back to this. Normally I show more self-restraint, but on the -- we can see on the screen that you, General, just said: "And it seemed as if everyone agreed with that status." Could you please give us the underlying facts, the basis, for this assessment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think there are some documents which I guess I will have to see if I can uncover here in these books which suggested that activities were normal in Prijedor and things were calm, and that people were getting along, even though there were ethnic differences among the population of that city/town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'd like now with the Court's permission and the usher's assistance to show you 65 ter number 308, and if it could be placed on the ELMO. It's dated 26th of May 1992. If we can scan so that the document in its entirety -- if we may scan so that the document in its entirety is shown on the screen. Thank you. Now, this, sir, is a letter from the local police chief Simo Drljaca again to his, as you call stove pipe chain of command, in the Banja Luka Security Services Centre. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, I would ask the technician to please focus on the last paragraph of this document so we may have it before us. This is, sir, a couple days after the events that transpired both in Hambarine on May 22nd as well as those that transpired on May 24th in the village of Kozarac. Specifically, can you read for us that paragraph, the last paragraph, that

utterances.speaker: MR. DRLJACA WRITES
utterances.text: "With respect to the activities that were organised," and I'd like to ask you who organised the activities based upon these documents?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: "Further activities in this regard will be carried out in an organised manner and in cooperation with military organs and members of the national security service. The intensity of these activities will depend on the development of the combat operations and their possible spreading to other areas, about which we will inform you in time."

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, in this document, Mr. Drljaca says that there's cooperation with the military organs and members of the national security service. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Yes, he does.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: From this or any of the other police documents, sir, that you reviewed, was there any indication whatsoever that the civilian, military, municipal -- strike that. May I restate the question. Sir, in the documents that you reviewed, was there any evidence whatsoever to suggest or infer, much less establish, that the local civilian municipal leaders were involved in any of the activities resulting from the three incidents or attacks that led to the army setting up detention camps in the spring and summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: I haven't seen any evidence that suggests that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me show you, because the Court asked you and you testified in connection with the hostilities or the period of time that was relatively peaceful, namely from April 30th through May 22nd, 1992, I'm going to show you a document which is our 65 ter number 297, which is dated August 4th, 1992. It has ERN number 00916569.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry. In order that we don't lose order, in fact, the document that was provisionally marked D101 is to a certain extent identical with S275, save that it includes a date, the 13th of October, 1992, and the DX is crossed out and it's open. Otherwise, it's the same content. You agree that we admit this as S275-1?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then the last document we would have, this would be, then, in fact D101 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is S251, this document. It's already admitted as S251.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's take care and first find out whether it's really identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Perhaps the Registrar could also check the previously marked -- I'm not somehow the Court identified it, but Defence 65 ter 316, we believe is S263. I believe the Court had provisionally marked it as D98.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I hope that during the next break, we can have an assessment of the real number of the documents. But please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: General, the document that we're reviewing now seems to be a response to the again as you call it the stove pipe analysis from Simo Drljaca from the Prijedor station to his commander in Banja Luka. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Specifically, sir, that letter I'd like to focus with the assistance of our technician on subsection (b). You mentioned the Serb -- essentially the Serb takeover on or about April 30th, 1992. In this document that Mr. Drljaca is responding to his commander, does he state anywhere there that there was -- who does he identify as the people who took over in Prijedor? Can you read that paragraph for us, to us.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: "The members of the active and the reserve police force, practically alone and without a fight, took over in Prijedor, sealed off the town, and organised the security of all vital structures." The police.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Now, tell us from a general sense of the review of the documents that you have, and I know you've broken down the binders, whether the hostilities continued during the spring and summer of 1992 in the Prijedor Municipality, and please identify for us the binder that you're looking at and some of the documents in which it may assist you in answering your question. Was there continued chaos and essential anarchy in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Up to the point where the police took over as described in the document we just read from, things were calm. But then after the May 22nd incident, chaos and confusion set in and hostilities developed, and there was actual combat actions and activities. And that is shown in various combat reports from the military, and it's I think also shown in some police reports that we reviewed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough to grab the binder which reflects -- and what number binder, is it, sir, in your binders of materials?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Let me find it here first. Probably going to be binder number 2. It's under "Military Reports and Efforts to Maintain Law and Order"; "Military Reports, Combat Reports, and Provocations"; "Military Reports, Croatian forces"; "Military Reports, Abuse, and Persecution of Serbs." And what do you want me to do at this point, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is that the binder, sir, that essentially shows that after May 30th, 1992, that in fact hostilities continued to be -- to continue to exist in the Prijedor Municipality all the way through and including and beyond September 30th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: That's correct. There are numerous combat reports here that point out that activities of that nature were being conducted and were continuing to be conducted, and that hostilities erupted in and around the areas as a result of these activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, did you find from a review of these documents whether or not there were paramilitary formations that were created after May 30th, 1992, that resulted in criminal activity of both looting and burning of homes as well as killing citizens in the Prijedor Municipality?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Such elements, criminal elements, did develop, and they preyed on the citizens in and around the area, and their assets and their homes and their businesses. And these criminal elements were very active and very disruptive. And they had a very deleterious impact on the region. People were scared and fearful.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What was the effect on the morale of the military in the spring and summer of 1992 as a result of these hostilities that erupted and that continued to maintain throughout the spring and summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: The morale of the military was not at the highest level. I think that the regular members of military wanted to see action. They felt as if there was no action being taken. There was no leadership, there was no one in charge. And they wanted more activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Were there paramilitary formations formed by one ethnic group or all ethnic groups from the materials that you reviewed and found?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Actually, they were from all ethnic groups, including the Serbs, and some of them were criminal elements, in fact, even though they were paramilitary.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: From the documents that you reviewed, did the military from time to time attempt to repel or arrest the element -- the criminal elements, namely the paramilitary formations, regardless of what the ethnic background was?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: No, I didn't see any evidence of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did the paramilitary units that were considered in one document that we'll get to in a second as SDS extremists, and that would be the Serbian democratic party, as you know, the Serbian paramilitary unit, did they in conjunction with the military commit these crimes or did the military from your review of the documents complain about these criminal elements that existed in the Prijedor Municipality in the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: No, the organised military complained about the marauders in the area, the people who were out of control and the people that were just travelling the countryside and performing criminal acts. They were out of control and they were beyond the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, whose responsibility was it to attempt to arrest, investigate, interrogate, and ultimately charge these paramilitary formations that were looting, plundering, burning, and committing terrible criminal acts within the Prijedor -- terrible criminal acts within the Prijedor Municipality in the spring and summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: In my estimation, it would be the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to show you another exhibit with the Court's permission and the assistance of the usher, a newspaper article that is within your binder. Here it is, sir. And we do have copies actually for the Court. This is an article, while we are waiting for it to be placed on the ELMO, that appeared in Kozarski Vjesnik on the 9th of April, 1993, and it's an interview, I believe, with Mr. Simo Drljaca. And if I could direct the usher to turn to page 2 of that article which bears the ERN number 00389284. And we're going to focus on the last paragraph of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This would be D99, because, in fact, the previous marked D99 was S263.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic has an extra copy for us. We haven't received our copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, if the usher would be kind enough to, with the Court's permission, give a copy to the OTP. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Again, as I stated, we're directing our attention if I may to the last paragraph on the second page of this article, which discusses the cooperation between -- if I can read it, Your Honour, I know everyone can. "The cooperation between the civil authorities and the police station was satisfactory during the period of the seizure of authority. Everyone did his job. After the takeover of authority, however, the new people did not understand the real role of the police. The attempt to transform the police into a council body, which would execute orders given by the council civil authorities was unacceptable and misunderstandings arose." Obviously the article continues. General, my question to you here as it related to the prior document that we reviewed where Mr. Drljaca contemporaneous with the events that transpired in the spring and summer of 1992 states that the military -- I mean the police practically alone took over power, and then in his interview approximately one year later in Kozarski Vjesnik where he says there was cooperation. My question to you, however, sir, Mr. Drljaca even one year later clearly states that the police in essence, does he not, in essence would not and did not take any instruction or orders from the civilian authorities. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Correct. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: From the review of any of the police documents that you saw, sir, was there any indication that the police ever issued a report to the municipal civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: I never saw any such exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you at any time from your review of the military documents, including the daily brief sheets as I think they are called, from the military, was there any indication that those reports were being issued or copied to the civilian municipal authorities?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, let's talk about reporting for a moment. Can you tell me what the purpose of reporting is and providing information to people, and to whom such information should be provided in the context of your stove pipe analysis?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: In the military reporting and its purpose, it's probably like everywhere else, to keep all interested parties informed as to the situation, anticipated actions, condition of the organisation. And that reporting travels up and down the military channels. And the people that are involved in reporting try to make it as accurate as possible so that good decisions can be made based on those reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And sir, those reports, both from the military and the police, they would be considered somewhat confidential, would they not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Yes, in some cases they are confidential or even secret, depending on the content. But certainly, they are kept within the confines of the stove pipe.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: From the documents that you reviewed, was there ever a distribution list for any of the documents that would somehow find their way into the municipal, civilian authorities' offices or desk?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What's the significance, if any, of that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: The stove pipe was being maintained. It's a manifestation of the fact that the civilian authorities had no control over the military, and the military had no interest in informing the civilian authorities of their actions and activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, that opinion is it not based upon a reasonable degree of certainty?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And it's based upon your review of all the materials that you have before you, as well as your experience, education, correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you, sir, let's turn back to the detention centres for a moment, if you will. You viewed with me and without me videotapes of some activities within the detention centres. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, in those detention centres, as you've read from the fourth amended indictment and saw there were some very terrible things that occurred to many people within the detention centres, were there not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Apparently so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, that's not -- your opinion is not one saying that those detainees who were beaten, killed, or other crimes that occurred upon them, unfortunately, your opinion is not that that was justified. Correct? In fact, your opinion is that that was not justified, is it not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Those criminal activities are totally unjustified.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your opinion with respect to the detention camps, sir, is in fact the detention centres themselves, the camps themselves, were authorised to be established and in a time of conflict such as the three incidents that occurred in the Prijedor Municipality, that they were justified in opening those, detaining individuals, interrogating them, and holding them until, as Article of the Geneva Convention states, until cessation of all active hostilities. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Who, sir, from your review of the documents and your review of the tape, as well as the materials included in the articles that you've reviewed, who was in charge of administering, maintaining, and operating the detention centres?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: The military.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The Geneva Convention, sir, also provides that food, as you've highlighted somewhat for us in your report and your testimony earlier today, provides that food be provided to the detainees. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, from your review of the military documents, the type of food that was provided to the military, what type of food was it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: It varied. There were periods of time when it was what they described as hot rations, and then there were periods of time when it consisted of liquid food which I presume was probably soup.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that, sir, is reflected in the documents that you have in front of you, correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's found specifically in the military reports, both on the daily as well as the weekly summaries provided within the military chain of command. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you have an opinion based upon a reasonable degree of certainty with respect to the atrocities that happened within the camps, including the beatings, any rapes, and the killings that occurred, whose responsibility was it to punish -- first, whose responsibility was it to prevent these activities from proceeding or commencing?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: The commander is always responsible for all that happens or doesn't happen. So the camp commander is the first one in the line of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And now, sir, based upon a reasonable degree of certainty, your education, experience, as well as your review of the documents that you have before you, do you have an opinion as to who is responsible to punish the perpetrators of those crimes that existed in the camps in the summer of 1992 in the Prijedor Municipality?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Since those camps were maintained, operated, and administered by the military, it is within the purview of the military to take action against the criminals that ran the camps and allowed those atrocities to take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And now, sir, the camps, as you stated earlier today, were run, maintained, operated, and administered by both the military in conjunction the police. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Objection, that misstates the evidence and counsel is leading the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us from your review of the documents who it is in addition to the military that maintained, operated, and administered the detention camps in the spring and summer of 1992 in the Prijedor Municipality?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Is the question who in addition to the military?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: The answer is the police, the law enforcement people.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And with respect to that, sir, the crimes that may have been committed by either the police or the military at these detention centres, who based upon your opinion, has the obligation to prevent those crimes from happening?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Objection, the witness has already answered that question. Said it was the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It was slightly different because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think the question is indeed slightly different, and it comes down to the question whether the military would have any possibility to prevent the police from acting in this way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The answer is still the military. The military is in the final analysis, in my opinion, responsible for the operations of those camps. And even though it may be reinforced with elements of police officers, those police officers must come under the instructions and the direction of the military camp commander. They can't go off and do their own thing, like shooting people. And so it's still the camp commander and the military that's responsible.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: From your review of the documents, sir, did the civilian authorities ever obtain any written information from either the police or the military as to the activities that were occurring in the camps, specifically the perpetration of any crimes that existed in the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: I did not see any evidence of that in the documentation I reviewed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: At any time, with respect to the police and military in these detention centres who may have perpetrated crimes, were the civilian authorities obligated, namely the municipal political leaders, obligated to punish any of those individuals or does that stay within the purview of the military and the police based upon your stove pipe analysis?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Stays within the purview of the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have several other documents, and I'd like to introduce the documents that are reflected in the General's report as the footnotes that I believe he has. I just don't want to say I have no further questions unless the Court wants me to put the specific documents, because there's in excess of 200 or so documents we would like introduced into as evidence. I'll proceed the way the Court wishes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The first right, of course, is to hear the submission by the Prosecution having, as I understand, until now no access at all to these as you call it footnotes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Correct. Well, we have been able to find some of the footnotes. I can't say that we haven't looked at any of them. I have no objection to proceeding as Mr. Ostojic suggests. There is a small chance that we would have an objection after reviewing it, but as the Court is saying generally, we don't object, even on relevancy grounds we don't object to the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If need may be, the rule is as outlined in the beginning of the case that a decision can be reversed. So therefore, I think it's not -- absolutely not necessary to go into details of these footnotes and only that they may be provided to the Chamber and Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In light of that, we have no further objections at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The trial stays adjourned until a quarter to 12.00 [sic]. And we can proceed immediately after this? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. May I ask in the meantime, any objections to the admission into evidence the documents D95A through D101A?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then therefore, in this order as previously marked, admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Unless the Court has anything, else, thank you, Your Honour. We would like to move into evidence the report of General Wilmot as well as the obvious references in his footnotes, if the Court would like, and we are providing copies -- as I stated earlier, we will provide complete copies of the footnotes that was referenced by General Wilmot as an exhibit. We would ask that it be incorporated obviously in his report and we ask that that be moved into evidence with the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Objection to do so with the caveat that the one or other point may be revisited and then reversed?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No objection. But perhaps could I suggest that we don't go through the marking of the footnotes and admission now because there is -- some of them may be Prosecution exhibits. The report, could we perhaps just mark that for the moment and deal with the footnotes later. Whatever Your Honour feels is appropriate, but I do note that some of the Defence footnotes are already Prosecution exhibits. It would take some time to go through and determine this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it facilitates the reading of the report when we make reference to the footnotes as such and regard them in principle as part of the statement. And as I take it, there are no objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So therefore, this report is, including the footnotes, admitted into evidence. You concluded?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I have one other point if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In addition, Your Honour, the Defence would request respectfully that the six binders of documents, some of which overlap with the footnotes, be introduced in as evidence pursuant to the 65 ter numbers that are reflected on each the documents since those were the documents that the General reviewed and relied upon in giving his opinions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Once again, I want to invite the parties first to have a look on these documents and then I expect comments on this by the parties. If there are any objections, then we would rule on this. But I think it's premature to act as a judiciary normally should do, act blindfolded, but not in relation to exhibits, please. Mr. Koumjian, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: General, can we agree that it's a fundamental principle of international law that civilians cannot be targeted for military attack.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Yes, I think it's certainly a fundamental principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, I want to go through all of your conclusions basically in your report, but just skipping ahead for a moment, I want to go to the incident at Hambarine. Is it actually your opinion based on what you reviewed that the response of the military in Hambarine as described by Defence Witness DD whose testimony you cite was an appropriate military response to the incident as you understood it?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: May we have the footnote citation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I don't know the footnote. It's helpful if you can make reference to the concrete page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: General, you read the testimony of Witness DD, do you recall that, the witness who talked about passing through the checkpoint in the morning?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And later going through Hambarine and seeing I believe he said 30 to 50 houses that he could see from the road that had been destroyed by tank fire. That's quite memorable testimony, isn't it? Do you recall reading that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, is it actually your testimony and your opinion as an expert as a former general in the United States army, that destroying 30 or 50 houses along the road with tank fire is an appropriate response to the incident that you described at Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: No, it's an overresponse.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So, sir, in your conclusions that you gave in your report, when you say -- talk about the Hambarine incident and say in number 3, page 51, "In the instant matter, the military was justified in responding with the use of force in the manner demonstrated." You do not mean to say that that attack was justified. You now agreed that that was a crime that happened, the attack on Hambarine --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Maybe I misstated it in my conclusions. What I meant to say was that they were justified in responding, but they certainly weren't justified in tearing down 50 houses in someone's village, no. That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Interpreting that incident in the way most favourable to the Serb forces, two soldiers were killed by members of a checkpoint. The testimony of Witness DD was that there were three people when he passed that checkpoint earlier that day, but let us presume that there were 10 people, 10 or 12 at the checkpoint. Would it be correct that the military would be justified in targeting only combatants, those individuals who had taken part or were taking part in hostilities against the military?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: The military asked that the people responsible for the attack be turned in, and so the implication in my mind is that they were looking for the two or three or four or whatever number of people that were actually involved in the attack and in the killing of the two soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did anyone ever make you aware that actually there was a Crisis Staff decision, a Crisis Staff order, published in the newspaper requiring the people of Hambarine to turn over Aziz Aliskovic and the other persons involved in that attack?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Yes, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you consider that or did you mention it in your report, the fact that the Crisis Staff had ordered the surrender of Mr. Aliskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me object to the form of the question, Your Honour. I think it misstates the evidence. That was not an order, it was a public announcement. And I would ask that the counsel give the General if he wishes on that issue on ultimatums also the military ultimatum that's referred to in the document that the General has who issued the same ultimatum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The second part of your objection is dismissed for evident reasons. The first part, I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can show the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, this would be helpful if we have to show some self-restraint in assessing evidence at this point in time. Therefore, it would facilitate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I can show the witness all the documents I refer to, but I will not finish tomorrow if I do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In this concrete case, I think it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, I'll going to read to you from Exhibit S389-1A. The third paragraph down reads: "The Crisis Staff hereby orders the population of Hambarine local commune and other local communes in the area, that is, all the citizens of Muslim and other ethnicities, to hand over the perpetrators of this crime, particularly Aziz Aliskovic and his group who are the direct organisers of this clash to the Prijedor public security station or the competent military organs by 1200 hours today, Saturday, 23 May. This crime has exhausted all deadlines and promises, and the Crisis Staff no longer can, nor is it willing to, guarantee the security of the population of above-mentioned villages in this area." It's quite clear, General, isn't it, that this says the Crisis Staff is ordering the population of Hambarine to turn over Mr. Aliskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I object to the form of the question. I would ask that the caption of the document also be identified and read into the record, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, counsel can go redirect and cover the documents, but it's not proper to bring up his arguments in the middle of my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think we have shown a lot of patience, and also in both directions. I think it's the appropriate form of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I just may state, Your Honour, with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No, please accept the ruling.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I am accepting the ruling, I just have another objection. If counsel can place it on the ELMO so that we have the entire document. That was the procedure that was established with every one of our witnesses, I would presume. But fair enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In principle, it's for the parties to decide how they want to present, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Let me just, if the witness requests it, I'd be happy to do it. But it obviously will significantly lengthen the time for the examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: General, if you need to refer to any of these documents that I mentioned, I'd be happy to give you a chance to do so. I believe you're reading the transcript of what I read regarding this Crisis Staff order. Is it correct that in your report, you do not mention that the Crisis Staff ordered the population to turn over Mr. Aliskovic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you consider that fact in reaching your conclusions?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: No, in this case I don't think I considered that fact. Some municipal authority, in this case, published a notice and asked that the perpetrators of this crime turn themselves in. I see nothing wrong with that. I suppose that the authorities, the military, and the police, all at the same time were trying to get the attention of the population to bring this thing under control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, how do you order a population to turn someone over? Do you understand that? If I'm a woman living in a house in Hambarine with my children and my elderly parents, is it my responsibility to turn over Aziz Aliskovic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: No, I don't think so. I suppose in some instances where we offer rewards, then it might happen. But probably by just announcing it, it probably won't happen because people are going to be protected and people don't want to get involved and people don't want to be implicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Is it proper, then, to attack these people and destroy their houses with a bombardment that according to your report lasted six or seven hours? Is that a proper response --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: No, that's an overresponse.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, you talked about the camps, and I believe you testified today on the LiveNote that I had. It's page 76, line 1 or 2, that "the military was the one that organised and operated the camps," and you were asked earlier if the civilian authorities had a role in setting up those camps. And you said: "I haven't seen any evidence to suggest that." Am I correctly summarising your views?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, did you -- are you aware of any statement by Dr. Stakic that the civilian authorities set up the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that. And I wouldn't understand the definition of "set up" unless you explained it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If you heard -- well, Dr. Stakic say that these camps were a necessity of the moment, Omarska and Keraterm, and were set up on the orders of the civilian authorities, would that change your opinion as to who initiated the setting up of those camps?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: I'd have to know the definition of "set up." Do you mean he simply turned over some property to be used so a camp could be established? What does that mean, "set up"?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay, let's say he used the word "established." Let me withdraw the question. Let me ask another question.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, if the Crisis Staff -- if someone said that "no one can be released from this camp without my permission," would you understand that that person had a role in the camp?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: If the Crisis Staff said that no one can leave this camp without my permission --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Let me rephrase my inarticulate question.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
