utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, have you seen the order of the Crisis Staff that no one may be released from the Omarska, Keraterm, or Trnopolje camps without their permission?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: No, I don't think I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And certainly, you would not give the same testimony that you gave this morning if you had been aware of that decision. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: I would first have to have that refined a little bit and find out if anyone actually did leave a camp, the camps, without the permission of the defendant. In other words, he may have said it, but does it apply? Does it work? Is it operative? Is his word a rule?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, what evidence do you cite, do you have, that indicates to you that it was only the military that decided to set up the Omarska and Keraterm facilities?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: I don't think I used the word "set up," I think I used the words, something like operate, maintain, administer the camp. The setting up of the camp seems to me to be a different issue. It seems to be an issue of someone selecting a piece of ground and saying set up the camp there. I don't know if the military did in a or not. I didn't even care about that. I was only interested in who operated and maintained and administered the camp once it was established. It could have been set up by a civilian authority. I don't know. In fact, maybe that's exactly what did happen because what we're talking about here I suppose are facilities that belonged to somebody or some agency prior to the combat taking place. There are buildings involved. Someone must have owned those buildings. Who had responsibility for those buildings? Who selected those buildings? It could have been the political authority for all I know. The point is once they were set aside to be used as a camp, then it was the military that ran them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, what information do you have to show that it was the military that decided who would be detained or the military that ran the camps at Omarska and Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Well, certainly it's outlined in the doctrine of the military that that's exactly how things are to proceed, and so I relied on the doctrine. I relied on the rules and I relied on their procedures as the evidence that would strongly suggest that that's how it took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, if you became aware that the commanders of the camp were Zeljko Meakic for Omarska, an active-duty police officer, and Mr. Sikirica, police officer, for the Keraterm camp, would that change your opinion?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: No, because I saw evidence where the police and the military in conjunction with each other did run the camps. So I knew that there was police involvement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Let's go, sir, back to -- start from the beginning for a moment and talk about how you prepared this report and your background. First, I understand you have a very rich history in military history, military employment, and in the business world. Can you tell us what your knowledge was when you started this project about Prijedor and the former Yugoslavia. What experience and education did you have regarding Prijedor and the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Certainly very little about the local area you identified as Prijedor. But I did have I guess some working knowledge of the situation in this part of the world simply by watching the normal newscasts and occasionally reading an article or a news item about activities here. But I'm not a historian, and I wasn't focussed on this area. I was living my life doing other things and had other work to do. And I think it was simply sort of a background sort of thing that I was observing and watching as one watches current events.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In fact, in 1992, if I understand from your curriculum vitae, that you were involved in three different businesses, one being the construction, one being the business out of London, and I believe there's a third one that perhaps you could remind me of.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Maybe doing some consulting. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Perhaps. So that would be correct as far as what you were doing in 1992. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Generally speaking, I think that's about right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You cited what you looked at in preparing your report, and recognising that we have an awful lot of documents in this case, can you tell me, have you reviewed the Prosecution exhibits in this case, reviewed all of them, some of them, and if only some of them, how were they selected?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: I did review some of them. I reviewed the materials submitted by your military expert, Mr. Brown, and I reviewed his testimony. So I did look at that document that he produced, his military report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us if you saw any factual errors in Mr. Brown's report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: No, I don't think I saw any factual errors. In his cross-examination, I see where he and I agree on many points concerning the events that took place at the time. So there was compatibility, and essentially I think we agreed on the doctrine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, you indicate in materials reviewed, that you reviewed, academic historian reports, you mentioned Mr. Donia and Mr. Trifkovic, I believe, this morning. Was there a third report that you reviewed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Well, certainly General McKenzie, I considered him to be in that category. I think there was a third one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you actually read General McKenzie's book diary or only the exhibit that was shown today?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: No, I read excerpts. I didn't read all the material. It seemed like there was a considerable amount of material to try to digest, so I didn't read it all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You were given certain documents to read by the Defence and were given by the Defence transcripts of certain witnesses. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And it would be correct that this was selected by the Defence team, not by yourself.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: No, I think it was a combination. The first thing I looked at was the indictment, and from the indictment I thought -- I sort of created an outline in my own mind of what I wanted to see and what I wanted to understand and what I wanted to know, and so I asked about a series of documents where I could get that information. Those documents were provided. And then they were enhanced on the recommendation of the Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned this morning a report by Mr. Butler. Which report was that that you reviewed? Sir, may I just suggest -- I have a document to be distributed. Perhaps you can just tell us if this is the report.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: You have the very report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: While it's being distributed, could I you, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry, before it's distributed, you don't see any obstacles?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: This is a report from the Krstic case, it's a public document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You refer only to the Krstic Butler report but not the November report?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Then I have no problems with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, this is the report that you reviewed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Why is it, sir, that you didn't cite that among the material that you reviewed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Because it was reviewed late, so I didn't identify it as one of the reports that I had reviewed. It came to me late.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: After you wrote the report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Actually, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Are you sure about that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: I think so, yes -- no, maybe you're right. I think you are right. I believe I was here about four weeks ago, and I think on -- during the flight back to the States, I did go through this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, if I would suggest to you that beginning on page 16 of your report through page 28 of your report, you basically have just summarised --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: What's in Butler's report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: -- what's in Mr. Butler's report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Yeah, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Without citing him.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Is that significant?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, sir, as an author, do you find it significant, do you find it ethical to take a paper from someone else, submit it into an international court as your own work without citing it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: I see what you mean. So you're talking about plagiarism, which it looks like I'm guilty of here. And to Mr. Butler, I would apologise immediately. But you are right. This is a lift from Butler's report, and yes, it's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Sir, if I understand, the fundamental tenet of your stove pipe analysis is that a single civilian was at the head of the army, that being the president of the federal republic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: The president and a secretary of defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, in April 30th, 1992 -- let's even go back. Let's go back to 1991. At the time of the outbreak of hostilities in Croatia between the JNA and Croatian forces, who was the president that headed the army that you're talking about, the JNA?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: I believe I have his name here somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If I could help you, I don't believe it's in your report.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: No, it's not in the report. I thought I had an annotation, but go ahead and help me if you could.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Go ahead, I'm sorry. If you can find it.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Was it Radovan Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, actually Mr. Karadzic was a Bosnian Serb. I'm asking who was the president of the federal republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: I don't know it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You've heard, I'm sure, of Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: I certainly have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you think Mr. Milosevic who was not the president of the federal republic of Yugoslavia had any influence on the military, if you have any knowledge of this, in 1991 at the time of the war in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I object to the form of the question, Your Honour. I think it goes outside the scope of the direct and this is obviously an attempt by the Prosecution again to obtain evidence for other proceedings that they have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No, it's certainly not. I can withdraw it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I can't see some merits in this objection at all, so therefore, please proceed, Mr. Koumjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: From your layman's knowledge of the former Yugoslavia, did Slobodan Milosevic have any influence on the JNA?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you hear that a large number of generals had been retired, forcibly retired from the JNA, by Slobodan Milosevic prior to the outbreak of hostilities?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, that actually under your stove pipe analysis in 1991, Stipe Mesic was the president of the federal republic of Yugoslavia. I don't know if you're familiar with that name, are you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you recognise that he is now the president of Croatia, and following your analysis, the current president of Croatia ordered the JNA to attack Croatian forces. Wouldn't that be illogical, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: I created the stove pipe analysis and the idea of the stove pipe only to show a doctrinal issue, to highlight a doctrinal issue which is that an authority at some local level doesn't have any influence on the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What I just told you that that analysis is absolutely not appropriate for the former Yugoslavia at that time. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: No, I don't think so, because I think you're talking about a very senior or a significant civilian authority as opposed to someone in some municipality or city like Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, sir, it's actually from your report on page 9, the second full paragraph where you said: "Having said that, it is fully understood that in Yugoslavia in 1992, at the very highest level, there was a civilian authority who exercised command and control over the army, the president of the nation." But you don't know who that president was, and you now agree that that person did not have control over the army. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: I don't know who that person was, and as I said earlier, I was only trying to describe a doctrinal issue and not one that was in practice at the time or in practice in this situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: On the 30th of April, 1992, do you know whether the army in Prijedor was the JNA or the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: It was the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Actually, sir, it was still the JNA until the VRS was created the 12th of May or in early May. So would it be correct that on the 30th of April, if I am correct what I just told you, that it was the JNA that was in -- let me withdraw the question. Sir, at the time of the attack on Hambarine and Kozarac, it's correct that the VRS was the -- was created, had been created. Can you tell me who commanded the VRS at that time, what civilian was in charge?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: No, I don't know who the president was at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: But it's clear to you that there would have to be a single authority in command. Is that right, under the stove pipe?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Yes, there had to be a single authority in command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Have you heard of the collective presidency in the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: On the 30th of April, 1992, do you know who the -- how many presidents there were of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Was it seven?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No, there were two actually. Biljana Plavsic and Nikola Koljevic. Do you know which of those if either exercised control over Serb forces at that time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, the 30th of April, 1992, you talked about the Serbian takeover. And in your report, you call it a peaceful occupation. Was it peaceful, sir, because of those who took power or because there was no resistance?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: It was peaceful because there was no resistance. It seemed as if the authorities came in and said, Here's what we're going to do, we're now a Serbian community, and there was no resistance to that. So it was peaceful. It takes two to have a conflict, and that didn't occur.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, would you describe the -- Hitler's occupation of the Sudetenland or the Soviet occupation of Czechoslovakia in 1968 as a peaceful occupation because there was no resistance to those occupiers?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you understand that in Prijedor early in the morning, police and military forces set up checkpoints, took over the Municipal Assembly and other key buildings, turned the elected president of the Municipal Assembly out of his office, and took power by force of arms? Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: I'm not sure if that is exactly what happened or not. Maybe I haven't seen that document where that evidence that you suggest is there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And please, I don't mean to be insulting to you because I realise that you had a limited amount of time to review the documents. Sir, did you ever review an interview, a radio interview, where SDS leaders and military officials talked about the takeover of Prijedor on the 30th of April 1992?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you know what the Territorial Defence is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: I think it's referred to as the TO, is it not commonly referred to as the TO? And I understand that it's leftover from the days of President Tito, and it's sort of like a reserve or national guard organisation that can be called up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Would you describe that as military?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Once it's called arms, it becomes military.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, I don't know if you're familiar, are you familiar with the name Slobodan Kuruzovic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If you were -- review -- well, I'm not going to try to prove the case over again to the witness. Let me move on to another subject. I just want to go back for a moment to these footnotes. I believe it was 70 and 71 in your report. When you wrote your report, had you read the exhibit that's now in evidence from -- regarding General McKenzie?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: I read excerpts from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Would you consider General McKenzie an academic historian?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: No, I don't think he's an academic historian, but he was a person on the scene apparently, in country.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Correct. But you would not call him an academic historian.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: No, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Why did you call in your footnote, cite various accounts presented by academic historians if you were relying upon General McKenzie's article or diary?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Because I had 30 hours to try to put this thing together, and so there are some footnote errors which I will readily admit to, and some typographical errors throughout the report, and I just did the best I could, I guess. So maybe I misstated what he was or thought he was something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, you began -- you began this morning by talking about the importance of presenting both sides to a conflict.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And I believe on page 2 of your report, the last paragraph, you say that "this is important to avoid the presentation of a distorted, biased, prejudiced view of the events. It is my view that this report gives a balanced and objective overview of the events." Footnote 71 of your report appears to be from a Tanjug news report. Do you know what the Tanjug news service is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In trying to understand and present an accurate history of events, particularly in a brutal civil war, do you think it's important to look at the source of the information that you've received?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Of course it's important.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Tanjug news service, if you knew this, that it was a news service from Belgrade, and at the time this article was published, 1996, that Belgrade, as you know, the then president of Serbia was Mr. Milosevic. And do you believe that this article is worthy of being cited as an accurate account as to the number of persons killed in this incident in Tuzla that you cite?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: I guess what you're suggesting is that the article is biased and prejudiced. It's like a "New York Times," "Washington Post" issue, I guess. So you're saying that maybe the report is not accurate. Well, in the time frame I had to put this together, I took reports and I didn't check out the accuracy or the political inclination or the -- whatever background was associated with the news agency or the newspaper or the television station. And so I simply took it on face value.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, you have a short section reviewing the events leading up to the conflict, and you talk about the attack on the convoy in Sarajevo, and this attack that you talk about in Tuzla. Apparently you did read the "Death of Yugoslavia" or reviewed the videotape of that. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Yes, I reviewed some videotape and got a feel for it from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you recall in that videotape the interview of Mr. Jose Maria Mendiluce where he talked about passing through northern Bosnia, northeastern Bosnia, Zvornik, after Arkan's, I believe, troops had entered, seeing trucks with blood dripping from the back of the trucks, and discussing the aftermath of the bodies he saw of the occupation of Zvornik by Arkan's troops? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you remember from the video the peace demonstration in Sarajevo and the Serb snipers from the Holiday Inn hotel firing on the crowd, I believe a couple of people were killed that appeared in that video, they actually had footage of part of that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: I did note in the video that there were snipers and there was firing taking place, and at the time, I wasn't sure who the snipers were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Actually, it's quite clear that in the Holiday Inn video, it was the SDS -- that was Radovan Karadzic's headquarters at the time, and the video, at least according to the authors of that video, it was quite clear that those were Serb snipers. Isn't that true, or you don't recall?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: I don't really recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In presenting both sides of the conflict, can you point out in your report where you mention any attack by Serbian forces on non-Serbs in this section on the history leading up to the attack?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: I don't think I talked about any Serbian forces attacking in the history part leading up to the three incidents in the Prijedor area. But I do talk about the, of course, the attacks by the Serbian forces in those areas, and I do proclaim the overreaction of the Serbian forces at several of the instances that occurred which are mentioned in the report. So I understand that the Serbian forces did in some instances exceed the bounds of normal military operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What incidents do you mention in your report other than saying that there were paramilitaries out of control? What incidents do you mention in your report committed by Serb forces? And let's specifically talk about -- well, let's talk about all of Bosnia, anywhere in Bosnia including Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: It's possibly not in the report, but I think I mentioned in testimony this morning about that neighbourhood village area, the suburb of Prijedor, where there was certainly an overreaction. And that whole entire area was apparently decimated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. That was Stari Grad.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Stari Grad, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, were you aware of the Room 3 massacre at the Keraterm facility?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Now, do you believe that that was done by someone out of control? Do you have any evidence to suggest that the military does not know -- did not know at the time exactly who it was that perpetrated that crime?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: I would imagine that the military does know who perpetrated that crime, and I think in my testimony I suggested that those kinds of crimes must be -- must be investigated and the people involved must brought to justice. So I certainly don't condone that sort of attack in a Detention Centre or a camp or whatever you want to call it. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned that even the lowest private would have a duty to report such a crime.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you think the president of the municipality would have a duty to condemn such an act publicly and to bring it to the attention of whatever authorities could punish or prevent those types of crimes?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Object to the form of the question, Your Honour. I can state my reasons if the Court wishes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In the moment, I can't see any reason, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the fourth amended indictment does not make an allegation against Dr. Stakic that he failed or breached any laws and that it is a crime not to condone an act. So for him to suggest that by virtue of the fact that Dr. Stakic did or did not condone an act such as the Room 3 massacre --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You need not continue because the question was, of course you could discuss the first part of the sentence, but to bring it down to the point is the question whether it was to the bring it to the attention of whatever authorities what could prevent or punish those types of crimes, and this, no doubt, is one charge in the indictment. The question of condone, I think is a separate one. So if you could please be so kind and answer, especially the second part of the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That being: Do you think the president of the municipality would have a duty to condemn such an act publicly? Is that the question I am to answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: To bring it to the attention of those being responsible for the investigation, the punishment, or to prevent those types of crimes, as you can read it on line 21.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly he's responsible for, and he's responsible for it -- first of all, he's got to know about it. Was he aware of it? And then he's responsible for certainly doing something about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, as a person with particular experience in civil conflicts, because I know you had mentioned in being in combat in Vietnam and participating in actions in Afghanistan, is it correct that in a civil conflict, that there is much more than just a military aspect to all operations? There is a political aspect that everyone fighting such a war has to keep in mind? In other words, to use the expression that was popular during Vietnam, "to win the hearts and minds"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: I'm not sure of winning the hearts and minds is a political aspect from the soldiering aspect, but yes, there are other factors and other activities that are going on outside the military action that impinge on that action.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What effect do you believe it would have had in Prijedor if the president of the municipality had brought to light that the military was committing gross war crimes in its attacks on Hambarine, Kozarac, Stari Grad, and in what was happening in these detention camps where thousands of his citizens were being detained?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: I suppose the citizens of those municipalities could see what was taking place. They saw Stari Grad. They saw it decimated. I don't know that the president needed to say anything about it. It was there to be observed and to be seen. With regard to what was happening in the prisoner of war camps, I'm not so sure that he had the information available to him. I don't see any evidence to suggest that he does or did, so I don't know if he knew what was going on in those camps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not going to put all the evidence that we've heard over the last year to you. I understand you haven't had the opportunity to review it all. But let me just ask you this: If you were the commander of the VRS -- General Mladic, the president of the Municipality of Prijedor, made public statements saying the military in Prijedor is abusing the citizens of Prijedor, committing crimes, these commanders Arsic and Zeljaja will have to go, do you think that that would cause some reaction by the general in charge of the army?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I object to the form of the question, Your Honour. It calls for speculation and it's an incomplete hypothetical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Maybe it's appropriate to rephrase this question, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, you testified that the civilian president could have no effect on the military. My suggestion to you is that, in fact, a person publicly identified as the president of the municipality who would publicly condemn crimes committed by military forces in a civil conflict in his municipality, that that would have important repercussions and that the commanders of the army would have to or would be likely to respond to such a public statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Same objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This time dismissed because it's part of the Prosecution's case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If such a forceful statement were made, then I presume that the military commanders would investigate and look into the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: This would be an appropriate time if Your Honour wants to break, or I could go on for a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please go on a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us what you know, if you know anything, about the National Defence Council. Have you heard of that body before?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: I don't know anything about the National Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you review the minutes of the Prijedor National Defence Council, perhaps the fairest thing would be to show those to you at this time. If the usher could bring the witness S60 and S28.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: This is the municipal organisation, right? The name National Defence Council has thrown me off track. Yes, I did review some of the documents from the National Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you tell me, sir, what your understanding is as to why the National Defence Council was necessary, why such an organ existed in the former Yugoslavia and under the defence doctrine of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: It was probably created to -- it was probably created to keep the civilian authorities informed of what might be taking place within the Defence department or whatever it was called in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Have you heard of the doctrine of all people's defence?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Does that have to do with the TO organisation and how that's raised up and brought up?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, let me just ask, are you familiar with the word? I believe it goes beyond that.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: All people's defence. No, I'm not real -- I'm not familiar with that doctrine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, are you familiar with the fact that on the 22nd of May, there was a decision by Dr. Stakic to mobilise individuals, that all soldiers report to their units, all of the soldiers that were being mobilised?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Yes. This was a situation where mobilisation was being put into action, and people in the local areas were being notified that mobilisation was taking place and were asked to report to certain stations and facilities to make themselves known to the authorities apparently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if we could put S28, the first page, on the ELMO, please, and perhaps help you find your own copy. Sir, I'd like you to consider this document in relation to the separate, nonoverlapping chains of command that you talked about in your stove pipe analysis. You see that this is a decision signed by the president of the National Defence Council, Dr. Stakic. And this council was -- and I will inform you of the people's positions -- the members of the council were Dr. Stakic; among the members was Rade Javoric, who I believe was the former head of the TO; Slavko Budimir, who was in charge of the municipal secretariat for people's defence which had to do with mobilisations among other duties; Slobodan Kuruzovic, the new head of the TO; Milan Kovacevic, who had a civilian function; Vladimir Arsic, the commander of the 43rd Brigade; Simo Drljaca, the police chief, Bosko Mandic head of civilian function; and Radmilo Zeljaja, who as you know was the deputy commander at that time of the 43rd Brigade. Among the conclusions the first one has to do with reinforcing the TO, and a war unit, which I believe we've had testimony, 4777 is part of the 43rd Brigade; mobilisation orders in point 2, an order about public enterprises in point 3. Skipping over a few just to get -- point 5 has to do with securing priority communications. Point 6 is a curfew, first let me ask you about that. Do you understand that the curfew in Prijedor would be enforced by the police, the military police, and part of the military, the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Is that a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, from reading this particular decision and from what you know about how curfews are normally enforced, would you understand that the police, and according to this decision, the military police and the TO, would enforce the curfew?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: It appears as if the police and the military police and the Serbian TO organisation would enforce the curfew.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The seventh point deals with paramilitary units and individuals who possess weapons and ammunition illegally are being called upon to surrender them immediately. And it gives a deadline. The last sentence says: "After this period, the relevant organs will start searches and seizures of any such weapons and ammunition and will apply the most rigorous sanctions." From this document, particularly the last two points, sir isn't it correct that there appears to be significant coordination between the civilians, particularly Dr. Stakic, the military, and the police, and that decisions were made signed by Dr. Stakic and enforced by the military and police?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Well, were they enforced? Is there documentation that shows that enforcement did take place? Is this really coordination or is it simply cooperation. Dr. Stakic didn't have any forces at his command that I know of, and so it was decided to have a curfew. In order to have a curfew, you've got to have somebody that will enforce the curfew. So Dr. Stakic apparently, through his signature here, said they were going to use the military police to do that. But did the military police really do it? Did this information go to the military? Did they cooperate in this effort? I don't know. I see that he wrote a plan and an order and instructions, but I don't know what the result was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you have any information that would make you believe that this was simply wasting his time, that he wrote this order with no intention that it be carried out and with no authority to have it carried out?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: He could very well have an intention to carry it out, but I don't know that he had the tools, I don't know that he had the mechanism to carry it out. And in my limited investigation here, I haven't seen anything that suggests that he does that. If you can show me something, then maybe we'll be able to agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Trying to avoid showing you new documents, just going with what you've discussed in your own report. Sir, you saw a lot of evidence about weapons being seized and searches for weapons being done in Prijedor by the police and by the military. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So in fact there is evidence that this order was carried out. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: I don't know if they were responding to this order, sir. When the military was attacked at the checkpoint and at the roadblock, their response was to go and disarm people. I don't know that they are standing around waiting for Dr. Stakic to say: "Look, here's what happened here, you boys got shot, so you better go and -- in fact, let me write you an order. Let me write this order for you." I don't think that's the way it works. I think the military commander deployed his forces and went out and started chasing people. So I'm not so sure that this piece of paper ties to what happened. It may be an after-the-fact sort of thing where Dr. Stakic tried to make himself look good in the eyes of the public. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I appreciate that, you don't know. Sir, talking about the Hambarine incident, the information you have about the incident came largely from the testimony of Dr. Mujadzic, who was present shortly after the soldiers were killed. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Yes. I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And in fact, Dr. Mujadzic also pointed out that one of the persons at the checkpoint, a Muslim, was wounded. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Yes, I believe I recall that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Now, sir, I don't know if you've had any involvement - let me ask you - in investigating, for example, police shootings to see whether they were justified. Do you have any such experience in the military to see whether a shooting --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Would it be correct, sir, that just the fact that a police officer fires his gun does not mean that the shooting was not justified, was not proper? You're looking quizzical, so I'll try to make it --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: Please, try it again. I don't understand the question actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Police officers shoot people who haven't fired at them, quite often, I would say in the United States, and isn't it correct that just the fact that the police have shot someone, and even if they haven't fired at the police does not mean that the police were not justified? Let me try again, because my question is bad. Sir, if someone is pointing a gun in your direction and it appears to be of immediate threat, do you have to wait for them to fire the gun or are you justified in shooting at them to protect yourself?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WILMOT
utterances.text: If someone's pointing a gun at me and I have a gun, depending on the heat of that confrontation, I may choose to shoot them before they shoot me. And that's a personal viewpoint and that's a personal explanation of what might transpire between myself and somebody that's confronting me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: From the evidence that you reviewed, would it be correct to say that it cannot be determined by you or I exactly what happened during that shootout where one Muslim was wounded, two Serb soldiers were killed, and that it would take a very detailed investigation in order to determine whether the police at the checkpoint were justified in shooting the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me object to the form of the question, Your Honour, and also what police is he referring to? Is he talking about the members of the Muslim paramilitary that were at the checkpoint, and he should include for it to be complete, that two other soldiers were also injured, not just two killed, in order for it not to be a complete hypothetical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it is a good point in time to have a break. Before we break, please, are there any objections to the Butler report of the 5th of April 2000? This would be S425.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: My only comment is if the Court would like the entirety of the Butler report, that is only just one section of the report. The report spans in excess of 150-so pages. It's whatever the Court's pleasure is. That includes only just a section of the report itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We can only decide on that what was tendered, and only this part was for special reasons tendered. Do you have any other objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then admitted into evidence as S425. The trial stays adjourned until tomorrow, 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: at 1.59 p.m., to be reconvened on Friday, the 21st day of March, 2003, at 9.00 a.m.
